title: International law plainly forbids Iran's tolls in the Strait of Hormuz, but enforcement, not doctrine, is the real difficulty.
paragraphs: The attack on a merchant vessel in Omani waters revived a conflict that a fragile memorandum of understanding had been meant to end. Within days the United States resumed its naval blockade of Iranian ports and promised to increase economic pressure. The sixty-day period that the memorandum allowed for a final agreement on the nuclear question then expired without result. Iran has since made plain that it intends to keep impeding traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. It also means to collect service fees from vessels that pass, presenting the charges as a legitimate source of national income. The strait is a major waterway: roughly one-fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas once flowed through it. The dispute is therefore not a regional quarrel but a problem for the whole trading system. Accounts of what is actually happening there conflict: American commanders claim to have cleared mines, opened a protected corridor and moved substantial volumes of oil. Shipping analysts, by contrast, estimate that only about two-thirds of pre-war traffic gets through, and only with military protection, darkened transponders, fixed time windows and continuing exposure to drone attacks. What is not in doubt is that the situation is unstable and that international law, whatever it says, has not yet restored free passage.

The only part of the memorandum that appears still alive is the dialogue between Iran and Oman on the future administration and maritime services of the strait. The two neighbours, however, read the law very differently, and official statements reveal that the littoral states do not share a single view of what it permits. Oman affirms that it continues its transparent and neutral cooperation with all parties in order to restore freedom of navigation, in full compliance with international law. It remains committed to its obligations as a party to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The legal position is unusually clear, although the political one is not, which is precisely why the dispute is so difficult to settle. The convention governs straits used for international navigation through a regime of transit passage, conferring a broad right of navigation and overflight that bordering states may not suspend. That right holds even when security grounds are advanced, and the convention also prohibits tolls for passage. Charges are permitted only for specific services actually rendered to a ship at the request of its operator. Iran's demand for fees equivalent to five to seven percent of cargo value plainly conflicts with that rule. Its insistence that inbound traffic be routed through Iranian territorial waters and obtain clearance is open to the same objection. The same demand is equally hard to reconcile with the narrower regime of innocent passage that Iran itself invokes. A coastal state may regulate such passage, but it may not impose requirements whose practical effect is to deny or impair the right. Even before the convention was drafted, customary law barred states from levying tolls in international straits, and leading shipping organisations recently restated this principle in a joint letter to the United Nations and the International Maritime organisation. Compulsory charges, they warned, would set a precedent capable of undermining the legal framework for straits everywhere and of generating uncertainty for global commerce.

Iran might argue that its pecuniary demands rest on Article 43 of the convention. That provision calls on user states and strait states to cooperate by agreement in maintaining navigational aids and in preventing, reducing and controlling pollution from ships. The rationale is sensible enough: littoral states should not bear alone the cost of keeping a waterway safe and clean for the vessels of many other countries. The operative words, however, are cooperation and agreement, and the straits of Malacca and Singapore show how they are meant to work in practice. There, critical aids to navigation are financed by a fund built on voluntary contributions from user states such as Japan, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates. That fund is not a toll imposed on transiting vessels as a condition of passage; its resources are reserved for navigation aids and are not a general source of income for the coastal states. Article 43 is a burden-sharing provision, not a licence to coerce payments from ships; if Iran tried to enforce such charges, shipowners would find themselves between two dangers. Those dangers are Iranian demands backed by a demonstrated willingness to fire on civilian vessels, and American sanctions, together with the loss of insurance cover, that follow any payment.

The pressure is not confined to a single waterway, and the evidence of its spread is uncomfortably clear. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which was designed to bypass the strait, mark one line of advance. The success of the Houthis in gaining ground near Bab al-Mandab, another potential choke point for Gulf exports to Europe, marks another. Various other sites along the export routes could provide an alternative if the conflict continues. A senior Iranian security official has said that Hormuz will remain closed until his country's demands are met, including the release of frozen assets and an end to other regional conflicts. Any arrangement with Oman on the future administration of the strait therefore promises far less than its language suggests.

Using military force to reopen the strait looks less attractive than it once did, and not chiefly for legal reasons. Iranian attacks on commercial vessels are unlawful under the laws of armed conflict. They may also amount to an armed attack on the flag state, within the meaning of Article 51 of the United Nations Charter, if their scale and effects are grave enough. An armed attack triggers a right of self-defence, and other states may assist the victim under the principle of collective self-defence. The legal basis therefore exists, but the practical difficulty is that a campaign to keep the strait open would require a continuous naval presence and would thus expose allied shipping to further attack. Such a campaign would be more likely to raise insurance rates and oil prices than to lower them. Force can punish interference; it cannot guarantee the stable and predictable passage on which commerce depends.

That leaves a different approach: a set of measures which are slower, less dramatic and more durable than force. States whose vessels are attacked should record each incident carefully, publish the evidence and treat the cumulative pattern as a legal claim rather than as a series of isolated crimes. Flag states can coordinate escorts, share intelligence and press insurers and port authorities to refuse cover or service to vessels that pay unlawful charges. Diplomatic efforts should follow a patient process, concentrating on the littoral states that have kept their commitments, above all Oman. They should also seek to widen the group of user states willing to fund navigational services voluntarily. The aim is to make the payment of tolls costly and the refusal to pay safe. None of this will reopen the strait quickly, and none of it removes the risk of a wider war. But a rule asserted by many states, documented in public and supported by concrete costs, is far harder to abandon than a rule that is merely announced. International law rarely resolves a crisis of this kind on its own; it supplies the standard against which conduct is judged and the vocabulary in which a response can be organised. On Hormuz, that is still worth having.

title: A senator's biography of Justice Clarence Thomas and the debate over originalism
paragraphs: In August, Senator Ted Cruz published a biography of Justice Clarence Thomas, and the book reached the top of the non-fiction list. What separates the book from numerous third-party histories of the Court is the access behind it, since Thomas provided the senator with over nine hours of personal interviews. Cruz served as a clerk at the Supreme Court in the 1990s, later established a career as a legal professional, and now sits on the Senate Judiciary Committee. He has taken part in the process of confirming numerous federal judges, and that experience provides him with a view of the institution that few authors share. When he visited the justice's chambers earlier this year to propose the project, Thomas gave his accord at once, and his motive, as Cruz tells it, was personal. A law professor or a stranger would have been refused, but a former clerk with a public record on judicial appointments could indeed be trusted to relate the account.

The title of the book points to a principle that runs throughout Thomas's work on the bench: that the highest authority in a constitutional issue is the document and the original sense of the document itself. Among the nine justices, Cruz argues, Thomas is by far the most willing to reject a prior decision that he considers to be wrong. He has never accepted the view that a decision, once made, must remain because it is old. It is never too late to go back, Thomas has often said, or, as he prefers to put it, to go further. That position is not a minor issue of legal method; it is a claim about the whole structure of thought, and it accounts for both the respect he attracts and the attack he meets. His admirers treat such discipline as a merit. His critics treat it as a threat to security, since a court that reopens its own decisions can unsettle freedom on which numerous citizens have come to depend. The argument, therefore, is not about the quality of Thomas's thought, which even his critics concede is correct, but about the role that a judge's own principles should perform in a system of constitutional rule.

Cruz states one chief purpose of the project on the back cover of the book. A man so extraordinary, he writes, would indeed be venerated, and if he were liberal he would certainly be. Instead of law schools and elementary schools bearing his name, the public response is silence, and something worse than silence. Cruz evidently believes that such absence is an offense, yet he insists that Thomas himself is untroubled by it. The justice, he says, is a man of strength who knows what he believes and does not seek honor from others. A small scene is offered in support of this claim. Justice Stephen Breyer once asked Thomas whether he desired to talk to the law professors who were expressing hate for him. Thomas replied that he could not see why he should concern himself with what those people thought.

No area of the law has felt Thomas's influence more strongly than race, and Cruz returns to the issue repeatedly. He traces the argument to the justice's insistence that the Constitution does not recognize color. Its clearest expression, he suggests, came in the decision of 2023 that struck down the race-based admissions programs at the University of North Carolina. Thomas joined the majority, but he wrote separately, and he took the unusual step of reading his opinion aloud from the bench. The government, he wrote, demeans all its citizens whenever it places them on racial registers and makes race relevant to the provision of benefits or burdens. Cruz observes that the passage was drawn word for word from a dissenting opinion that Thomas had written twenty years earlier. That prior decision upheld the use of race as one factor in admissions at a state law school. The effect, however, has been to keep the question open rather than to settle it. The senator's conclusion is that generations of students, lawyers and judges will still be reading that argument long after everyone now living has died.

The further purpose of the volume is to relate a personal journey that, in Cruz's view, has no equal among the justices on the Court. In 1955, when Clarence was seven, he and his brother were sent to live with their grandparents in a rural community in Georgia. Their father had abandoned the family, and their mother could not raise two boys alone while holding full-time employment. The grandfather, Myers Anderson, was a man of discipline and duty for whom education came first. His own background was one of poverty and difficult conditions, and he had no formal training or skill in reading or writing. He was determined that his grandsons should obtain the education that he had been denied. He stressed the importance of learning and refused to accept any assistance from the government, even when he was barely earning enough income to survive. He believed that such aid would harm a family's freedom and undermine its sense of responsibility. He maintained a strict standard of conduct, and he never hesitated to work. He provided guidance, training and a model of effort. His attitude toward existence had a powerful influence on Thomas's character. When the youths were not at school they worked, helping him deliver fuel oil or labouring on the family property. Physical activity was thought a waste of time, and the only acceptable substitute for work was a tour of the library. That experience shaped his later thought and his attitude toward the law. Every discourse about Thomas's early period, Cruz writes, has its beginning and ending with Myers Anderson, whom the justice has described as the one hero in his life.

The Catholic religious belief of his grandfather led Thomas toward the priesthood, and he attended a preparatory seminary, where he was one of only two black youths. His fellow youths found various methods of showing that he was not welcome, and he was ignored and insulted. That experience, together with his doubt about the Church's failure to act on civil rights, made him challenge the decision. He entered a seminary in Missouri to complete his studies, but his time there was limited. On 4 April 1968, Martin Luther King was murdered, and Thomas observed his fellow youths celebrate the killing. That scene, Cruz suggests, had a more significant influence on the judge than any course he later took at Yale. A legal theory, on this account, is not simply a collection of concepts acquired through training; it is the product of a particular existence. Thomas put the point to the author directly, observing that almost nothing in his legal theory came from Yale or from scholars. It came, he said, from his background and the conditions in which he was raised.

The book is plainly a work of admiration rather than of detachment, and its image of the justice will not persuade those who already distrust him. Yet the argument inside it belongs to a broader controversy. If the meaning of the Constitution is fixed by the text, and by the sense it carried when it was adopted, then decisions resting on later social theories lose their authority. A whole range of settled expectations becomes open to question. Whether that prospect is a promise or a threat depends on where one stands, and the disagreement is not likely to be resolved by any single biography. What Cruz does establish is that the debate over the Court's direction is now conducted as much through the lives of the justices as through their opinions. That the most senior member of the Court should be the subject of such a book is itself evidence of how far the entanglement of law and politics has gone. The author is a senator who might one day vote on the justice's successor.

title: The collapse of Banco Master and the corrosion of Brazil's system of checks and balances
paragraphs: On a November night, federal agents stopped the banker Daniel Vorcaro on the tarmac of Sao Paulo's international airport as he prepared to board a private jet. He was initially detained as a flight risk, was charged months later with bank fraud, corruption and money laundering, and now awaits judgment. Less than a month before a national election, the collapse of his bank has become the most serious test of Brazil's political institutions in a decade. At first glance it looked like an ordinary financial scandal, and the figures alone were dramatic enough. The Central Bank ordered the liquidation of Banco Master, producing a loss estimated at roughly 47 billion reais, or some nine billion dollars. Roughly nine tenths of that sum was repaid to account holders and shareholders by the Credit Guarantee Fund, in the largest payout in the fund's history. Even so, the episode placed the country's financial system under considerable strain and raised awkward questions about how banks of this size had escaped close supervision for so long.

Yet the scale of the loss is not what makes the case so dangerous for Brazilian democracy. Since 2018, Banco Master had signed contracts to manage retirement accounts for state and municipal governments, universities and other public bodies. Investigators say that Vorcaro built a large network of economists, commentators, bureaucrats, politicians and judges in order to shield these operations from public scrutiny. Some of them were hired to vouch for the bank, while others, prosecutors allege, were openly bribed to allow questionable transactions to proceed. Where persuasion failed, the banker is said to have intimidated and blackmailed his critics, including journalists and public officials. The pattern describes a man who understood that Brazil no longer had three branches of government that check one another, but three separately purchasable points of veto. Buying access to all three allowed him to hedge against the state, and such a strategy could only work because the country's politics had become increasingly dysfunctional. The result was a political system that had been losing the capacity to restrain private power for a decade.

The shift began in 2016, during the impeachment of President Dilma Rousseff, when the Speaker of the House discovered that his procedural office could be converted into a sword hanging over the presidency. In Brazil, Congress executes the budget as much as it legislates, and congressional earmarks became mandatory. They rose from nearly 13 billion reais in 2017 to 61 billion in 2026, roughly a quarter of all discretionary federal spending. A president can no longer withhold them in order to discipline an unruly coalition, which means that the executive has lost its main instrument of control over the legislature. Public spending, therefore, has become the main currency of political loyalty at the federal level. Money that might once have gone to health, education or infrastructure now serves to buy support. The Supreme Court, meanwhile, legislates whenever lawmakers reach a standstill, at times overturning decisions that Congress has already taken. Judicial activism increased sharply under President Jair Bolsonaro, whose permanent conflict with the Court over pandemic policy and freedom of speech pushed the justices into a political role they have never abandoned. A weakened presidency, burdened by public debt and pressured by the other two branches, has little leverage to push policy forward. This tug of war has become a trademark of contemporary Brazilian politics.

The influence network that investigators have mapped is remarkable not only for its size but also for its range. On the political right, Vorcaro is said to have offered cash and luxury perks to several prominent politicians. Brazil's financial intelligence unit traced roughly twelve million dollars to an American fund that was managing the budget of a film about Bolsonaro. That sum included roughly one and a half million dollars, sent in September 2025 at the request of the former president's son, himself a senator and a presidential candidate. Leaked voice messages also appeared to show a prominent far-right congressman reaching out to the banker for what looked like political favours. On the political left, federal police allege that a senator who then served as Lula's floor leader received an apartment in Salvador and three and a half million reais. A state governor who later became Lula's chief of staff is said to have favoured the bank's businesses as early as 2018 by allowing public servants to take out high-interest loans. The evidence remains contested in every one of these cases, and no court has yet established the facts. The political effect, however, is not in doubt, because almost every section of the political class appears to have had dealings with the same source of money. Few observers, therefore, consider the pattern a matter of coincidence.

The gravest allegations concern the judiciary, where the evidence is also the most treacherous. One Supreme Court justice stepped aside from the inquiry in February, after the press revealed at least 35 million reais in payments linked to Vorcaro. The money had gone to a resort in which he held a stake, and he denies any wrongdoing. The son of another justice received a consultancy fee of 281,600 reais that was ultimately paid by the bank. A third justice, often described as Bolsonaro's nemesis, faces the most explosive claim of all, for the law firm of his wife signed a contract worth 131 million reais with Banco Master. Police recovered the banker's side of conversations with this justice, which suggest an unusual degree of intimacy between the two men. There is, however, no hard evidence that he acted on any of the banker's requests. The report containing that material was commissioned by a fourth justice, who took over the inquiry earlier this year and who previously served as Bolsonaro's attorney general. That justice, an Evangelical Christian, has since become a devotional figure at far-right rallies. Critics accuse him of using the case to weaken a rival faction and thereby to undermine the Court's legitimacy, which is precisely what the far right has long desired.

The irony is that the politicians best placed to campaign on the Court's disgrace are the ones most exposed by the same files. One presidential candidate keeps demanding the resignation of a justice. He has so far failed to explain how he came to receive money that should have funded a film about his own father. Lula himself does not appear to be implicated in the scheme. He nevertheless remained silent for months, apparently to avoid being dragged into a crisis that mostly affected the other branches of government. Only when the rift within the Court became impossible to contain did he demand that every file in the case be unsealed. It may be too late for him to take a decisive stand on yet another corruption scandal in an electoral season. His support for the investigation will hardly improve his standing in the polls, but it could produce revelations that change the outlook of the race. What matters more is the question that the affair leaves behind for the country's political class as a whole. Perhaps the deeper issue is not corruption itself but the structure of institutions that makes corruption so effective. If a weakened president is returned to office, his difficulty will not be merely preserving democracy in the abstract. It will be restoring a balance among institutions that a single banker found it profitable, and apparently easy, to buy.

title: What the protest art aimed at Ed Sheeran reveals about the politics of pop music — and about the limits of mockery as a political act.
paragraphs: One recent cartoon depicts Ed Sheeran serenading a missile with the opening line of his best-known song. It belongs to a small but conspicuous type of protest: the image directed at a pop star rather than at a government. Sheeran became the subject of such images after he removed the rapper Macklemore from his tour, apparently because Macklemore had made a speech in support of Palestine. Within a week, illustrators and internet users had produced a range of satirical drawings, one of which imagined the singer auditioning new band members in 1933. The performer has never claimed to be a political artist, and his audience has never required him to become one. Yet the moment he acted on a political judgment, he was treated as though he had always taken part in a debate he had spent a decade avoiding. The episode deserves attention, although not because it reveals anything unusual about one celebrity's character. What it describes is the awkward position of the popular musician who is expected to have a voice and is then punished for using it.

The commercial logic of the music industry pushes performers toward a carefully managed silence. A stadium tour is a business that must be welcome in dozens of countries, each with its own laws, its own local authorities and its own sensitivities about speech. The system that surrounds such a tour makes explicit demands. Sponsors have reputations to protect, promoters have licences to secure, and national governments take a keen interest in what performers say on stage. Under these conditions, any political statement becomes a cost, and the safest course is to claim that art and politics occupy separate areas of life. Sheeran has long presented himself in exactly those terms, insisting that his songs are for everyone and that he has no interest in telling audiences what to think. For a performer whose product is sold as universal, neutrality appears less like cowardice than like a reasonable professional decision. The result is a class of figures who are famous everywhere and accountable nowhere.

The objection to that position is that neutrality is itself a decision, and usually one that supports the powerful. A singer who declines to comment on a war still performs in the countries that wage it, and his silence is interpreted accordingly. This is why the charge of cowardice has followed Sheeran rather than the many artists who never had an opinion attributed to them in the first place. Removing a collaborator is an action; it produces an effect that can be observed, reported and judged. Had he simply said nothing, his critics would have had no event to describe. The distinction between speech and action therefore collapses here, since a cancelled appearance is both a statement and a fact. Those who insist that artists should remain outside politics rarely apply the rule to performers whose politics they share.

Protest art aimed at celebrities has a long history, and its record is mixed. Boycotts and refusals have an equally long record, and their effect has always depended on the willingness of audiences to bear a cost. Cartoonists find it easier to mock a visible figure than to explain an institution, and the pleasure of recognition encourages a certain laziness. The tradition of Black American ironwork, in which smiths in the South embedded West African symbols into gates and window bars, suggests a different relationship between craft and politics. There, meaning was carried by the material itself, by the act of making something that would outlast its maker, rather than by a caption attached afterwards. Contemporary protest images, by contrast, circulate for a few days and then disappear into the same stream that produced them. The difference between the two traditions lies in whom they address: an institution that can be pressured, or an audience that can only be amused. That distinction is easily lost.

Institutions manage political expression more quietly, and often more effectively, than any angry audience can. A museum that reverses its photography policy, or a government that orders a review of a museum's content, exercises control without ever announcing a ban. Public argument attracts attention, while administrative procedure does the work. Decisions of that kind attract far less notice than a singer's tour schedule, yet their effect on the range of available expression is considerably greater. Economic pressure works at the same level: a sponsor withdraws, a venue cancels, and the result is silence without any law being invoked. Control rarely produces a headline, which is precisely why it succeeds. The controversy over one pop star therefore sits within a broader pattern of managed speech, and it is the noisier part of that pattern that we notice.

There is also a question of what the pile-on actually achieves. A viral drawing gives its audience the sense of having taken a position at almost no cost, and that feeling may be the whole of its value. The artistic lampoons of Sheeran are clever, but cleverness is not pressure, and the attention they generate quickly shifts to the next target. The pleasure of shared contempt is real, and it explains why such images spread so fast. The target is chosen for its visibility rather than its responsibility, which is why the campaign rarely reaches the people who actually decide anything. There is little evidence that mockery of this sort alters the behavior of an industry, and none at all that it produces the result its authors intend. The risk is that protest becomes a branch of entertainment, consumed in the same way as the music it criticises. Whether that constitutes a failure of art or merely a limit of it is a question the genre has never settled.

Perhaps the deeper issue is the concentration of cultural authority in a handful of figures who never asked for it. We treat a singer's opinion as important because his songs are everywhere, and then we are disappointed when the opinion turns out to be cautious and calculating. A society in which one performer's decision could genuinely affect a war would be a strange one. A society that behaves as though it could is simply confused about where power lies. The demand for a political voice is genuine, and so is the disappointment when that voice is cautious; both feelings are reasonable, and neither is easy to satisfy. Celebrities are required to be braver than the institutions that employ them, and they are then blamed for failing a test their employers designed. The cartoon aimed at Sheeran is funny, and the anger behind it is understandable. But the more useful response would be to build institutions — courts, unions, newspapers, schools — strong enough that no single celebrity has to carry the burden of speaking for a cause. Then a pop star could sing about the shape of anything he liked, and it would not matter very much.

title: The regulatory implementation of domestic procurement preferences and its potential to undermine statutory purpose.
paragraphs: In practice, legislatures pass statutes when they want to revive domestic industry; agencies write regulations when they must make those statutes work. It is usually in the regulation, rather than in the law itself, that political ambition of this kind is quietly trimmed. For example, the Department of Homeland Security's final rule on personal protective equipment, effective in October 2026, is a case in point. The rule codifies how the department complies with the Make PPE in America Act, a provision buried in a much larger infrastructure statute. Its declared purpose is to sustain and expand domestic manufacturing of the masks, respirators, gloves and gowns on which the national response to a public health crisis depends. Officials describe the change as technical: the department, they say, is merely recording in the acquisition regulation the practice it has followed since 2022. That description is accurate, to be sure, and it is perhaps the main reason critics of the rule are uneasy. In other words, the compliance scheme now written into the regulation is considerably more permissive than the language of the Act, and the gap between the two will decide whether the law changes anything at all.

The Act itself sets out a general rule and then a series of exits from it. In any case, agencies are directed to buy equipment that is grown, reprocessed, reused or produced domestically, including its materials and components. In some ways, they are also told to sign contracts lasting at least two years plus any option periods, so that manufacturers can justify investment in new capacity. As such, alternatives are permitted where a product assembled abroad contains only American materials and components. When an agency relies on such alternatives, it must certify, so to speak, every 120 days that the immediate needs of a public health emergency make them necessary. In addition, further exceptions are recognised for articles that are simply not available, or that cannot be procured at American market prices. As it were, each of these provisions was a concession to procurement officials who warned that rigid preferences would leave them unable to equip the country during the next crisis. Each also creates an administrative route around the Act's central purpose, and the practical effect of the rule depends on how wide those routes turn out to be.

By and large, the public comments on the proposed rule show how sharply the question divided interested parties. Twenty-three comments arrived within the deadline, and several asked the department to define "component" and "domestic personal protective equipment" more precisely. As we know, the specific concern was nitrile butadiene rubber, the raw material from which nitrile gloves are made. That substance can plausibly be described as a crude rubber or latex. The federal acquisition regulation already lists crude rubber and latex as nonavailable from domestic sources. As noted above, commenters therefore feared that a generous reading of the exception would let agencies keep buying gloves produced abroad while claiming to comply with a law designed to stop exactly that. As mentioned earlier, they argued, too, that the definitions of foreign-assembled and foreign products were loose enough for goods manufactured offshore to be labelled domestic. If that were allowed, the argument ran, foreign firms would enjoy an advantage over the American manufacturers the Act was meant to protect.

In the end, the department declined every one of those suggestions, offering various reasons that deserve attention. They are the sort of reasons agencies give whenever they are asked to make a domestic preference bite. As already noted, first, the list of nonavailable articles is reviewed and amended from time to time. Writing specific references into the acquisition regulation would risk conflict with later revisions, so officials preferred to rely on the existing statutory framework rather than record a precise determination of their own. Second, as the case may be, the department rejected the claim that the nonavailability exception applies only to components used in American factories. The statute, it observed, expressly covers an item of equipment, or a component or material of it, that is or includes a listed material. To read the exception narrowly would contradict the plain text. Third, as the time comes, the department concluded that no revision of the definitions was necessary in order to address the availability of the rubber in question. Officials added that the rule leaves the statutory framework intact, so that nothing prevents a later administration from taking a firmer line.

Presented in this way, the department's approach looks like a modest exercise in legal craftsmanship. The regulation follows the statute, and the exceptions in the statute are real. Yet the cumulative effect is to place the burden of proof on those who want domestic production rather than on those who wish to avoid it. A firm seeking an exception need only point to a listing that is itself subject to revision, while a contracting officer who prefers to buy abroad has a range of defensible positions to choose from. The evidence suggests that the remedies available to an American manufacturer that loses a contract are limited and slow. The 120-day certification requirement, which sounds strict, is a paperwork obligation rather than a barrier to trade. History offers few examples of procurement rules that rebuilt an industry through periodic certification alone. What such rules can do is change expectations; expectations do influence where firms place their factories, but the influence is indirect, and it is easily reversed.

In the meantime, the economic case for the preference is straightforward enough. A country that cannot produce its own masks and gloves is exposed to exactly the kind of shock a pandemic delivers, when foreign suppliers restrict exports and prices rise sharply. Building a domestic base, however, means paying more for goods that other countries make cheaply, and that cost falls on local hospitals, on taxpayers and on patients. The department's own data and analysis accept as much, while arguing that the difference is a reasonable price for security of supply. A common objection is that a preference without a clear definition of what counts as domestic merely shifts production to the cheapest compliant location. Since the exemption for nonavailable materials covers the very inputs on which domestic glove production depends, the department contends, the practical result is likely to be a change in paperwork rather than a change in trade. Which view is right cannot be settled by reading the rule; it will be settled by the pattern of contracts awarded in the course of the next few years.

For now, none of this means the rule is worthless. Contracts of two years plus option periods genuinely reduce the risk of investing in a domestic production line. A department required to certify its reliance on foreign sources every four months can be held to account by Congress, by the press and by its own auditors. Small firms that supply components may win a more stable market, and the signal sent to investors is not nothing. The difficulty is that a rule which leaves every significant determination to later interpretation cannot by itself sustain the expansion of an industry. The real test will arrive, in the long run, during the next shortage, when officials must choose between the preference they have written down and the equipment they need immediately. Whether the Act then looks like policy or like a promise will depend far less on its text than on the decisions the rule deliberately leaves open. In short, that is the ordinary fate of industrial policy in a system that distrusts it: the statute announces a purpose, the regulation administers an exception, and the market waits to see which one prevails.

title: Industrial heritage and the politics of memory
paragraphs: In the winter of 1984 the coal industry of the north of England began a national strike that lasted a whole year and produced a complete defeat. The government of the day treated the conflict as a test of political power, and the communities that depended on the pits lost the argument. By the end of the century almost every site in the region had closed, and the local economy had lost its main source of employment and income. What remained was a landscape of empty yards, rusting equipment and a local population that had few skills of any other kind. Three decades later, a considerable number of those same sites have been reborn as museums, parks and centres for visitors. Local councils present them as a source of employment and as evidence of a proud industrial past, and the argument is not without merit. Yet the process raises a serious question about who controls the account of what happened in these places. History, after all, is never a neutral record, but a selection made by particular people for a particular purpose.

The economic argument for this sort of regeneration is easy enough to state, and it is widely accepted. A former industrial site that becomes a museum can attract several hundred thousand visitors a year and provide a hundred or so jobs. Those visitors spend money in hotels, pubs and shops, and the effect on a district that has few other resources can be considerable. Governments of every political colour have therefore treated culture as an instrument of economic policy, offering grants to restore old buildings and funds for the training of local people as guides. The logic behind such investment is that a region which has lost its industrial base must find something else to sell to visitors. In a district where the pit once provided nearly every wage, a record of the industry becomes, rather neatly, the only remaining product. Local authorities have therefore proved willing to provide the funds, on the reasonable assumption that visitors will pay to see the result. Whether the sums add up is a separate issue, and one of considerable difficulty, because the funds are public and the benefits are uneven. Several famous sites have required continuous support from the state, and a few have ended in complete failure.

The more serious objection, however, concerns not money but meaning, and it requires a careful answer from those who control the sites. When a national industry is turned into an exhibit, the political conflict that destroyed it tends to disappear from the account. Visitors are invited to admire the equipment, to descend into a reconstructed tunnel and to imagine a personal experience that nobody in the party has shared. The violence of the strike, the riot at the pit gate and the bitter division within the community are quietly removed from the official record. What remains is a sentimental image of a lost world: strong men, warm beer, brass bands and a local pride that had nothing to do with politics or power. Such a version of the past suits the government whose policy closed the mines, because it allows a political defeat to be regarded as economic progress. The community is encouraged to celebrate an inheritance while the economic and social arrangements that produced its poverty remain untouched. Former miners now serve as guides, often on casual contracts and at wages well below what the industry once paid. They perform the memory of their own trade for the benefit of visitors who have come, in the majority of cases, simply for a day out. There is a certain irony in this arrangement, and the individuals who perform the work are perfectly aware of it.

Not every project follows the same pattern, however, and the exceptions are instructive enough to deserve a place in the debate. At a museum in south Wales, the guides are former employees of the industry, and they were given complete control over the account. They describe the conditions of their own personal working lives, argue with one another in front of visitors, and refuse to pretend that the closure was natural. The result is a museum that feels less like a monument and more like a social club with a serious purpose. Visitors come away with a sense of the industry as a human experience rather than as a display of timber and iron. Where local communities have retained a real share of the ownership, the account tends to be more honest and the attraction more durable. The reason may be simple: people protect what they regard as their own possession, and they resent an official account of what their own personal history means. Involvement of this sort is difficult to arrange and expensive to maintain, which is precisely why it remains rare in practice. It also requires a degree of confidence that a community which has lost its principal employer does not always possess.

The difficulty is not confined to Britain, since the loss of industry has produced the same dilemma in various national economies. In the Ruhr, an immense industrial complex has been converted into a centre of culture that attracts millions of visitors each year. Yet the region continues to suffer from high rates of unemployment, and the centre has not replaced the wages that the industry once paid. Culture can add to a local economy, but there is limited evidence that it can carry one on its own for long. The point is worth stating plainly, because the desire to treat culture as a substitute for industry is strong among political leaders who need good news. A museum may employ two hundred people. The industry it replaced employed two thousand, most of them local men with few qualifications and no other obvious route to a decent income. When the two figures are compared, the difference in scale becomes obvious, and no amount of clever design can conceal it. The danger is that a society will convince itself that it has dealt with the loss of its industrial base. In fact, it has merely replaced a productive economy with a service economy that pays less and employs fewer.

On a bench near the entrance, an old man in a leather jacket sits and stares at the ground. He does not go inside, because he says he does not need a museum to remember what happened, since he was there. He points to a line of houses and says that the people who live there now are not the same people who fought the strike. They come from somewhere else and do not know the town as he knows it. He does not blame them, but he blames the ones who wrote the official account, because they made a whole way of life look like a mistake. He says that if you want to honour the dead, you should not hide the fight that killed them. You should tell the truth, even if it makes some people uncomfortable.

In the end, the question is not whether these places are pleasant to visit, but whether they tell the truth about what was lost. A visitor may walk through a clean and quiet room, look at a photograph, and feel sad for a moment. Then the visitor goes home, and the town remains as it was, with fewer jobs and less hope. The men who once worked underground are now old, and many of them are not well. But they do not want pity, and they do not want a story that makes their lives look simple or happy. They want the story to be told as it was, and that is not a matter of money but a matter of respect.

title: The growing judicial role in settling election disputes, and its costs for democratic legitimacy
paragraphs: The Supreme Court's latest intervention in a dispute over mail-in voting has revived a familiar argument about who ought to settle the rules that govern elections. In a brief, unsigned order, the justices refused to let the Postal Service carry out a new regulation governing mail-in ballots. The rule would have imposed stricter conditions on the return of a ballot by post. A federal judge in Boston had already blocked it, holding that the agency had exceeded the authority Congress granted it. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote a short concurring opinion, while Justice Samuel Alito, joined by Justice Clarence Thomas, dissented. The immediate result is modest, yet the case belongs to a much broader pattern that has been building for decades. Something similar occurred in 2000, when the outcome of a presidential election turned on a single state's recount and five justices resolved the dispute. Election law has migrated from the state legislature and the local council into the courtroom, and there is little evidence that the movement will slow. The effect is that judges, rather than voters or their elected representatives, increasingly determine the conditions under which citizens cast a ballot.

Legal experts point to three developments that have sharply accelerated this trend within a single election cycle. The first is a Supreme Court decision that weakened the Voting Rights Act of 1965. That law had required certain states and counties with a history of discrimination to obtain federal approval before altering their electoral arrangements. Once the requirement was removed, several Southern states drew new maps within weeks, and some of those maps were immediately contested. Second, political leaders press the states they control to redraw boundaries for partisan advantage, and the opposing party responds in kind. The third is a series of new voting rules, from stricter identification requirements to limits on mail-in ballots, that are challenged as soon as they take effect. Taken together, these forces have turned what was once a periodic activity into a continuous one, sustained by well-funded organisations on every side of the argument. Litigation of this kind is expensive, and the organisations that bring it are, for the most part, well funded. The volume of cases therefore reflects resources as much as it reflects genuine uncertainty about the law.

The available data suggest that the volume of election litigation has reached a level without precedent in modern times. Analysts describe the current figure as well above historical norms, particularly for a midterm election, when the courts are ordinarily less involved in the administration of voting. The underlying question, in each instance, is how far courts may go in supervising an activity that the Constitution assigns, in the first place, to the states. One dispute concerns an attempt by the federal government to obtain access to a database of immigration records. Officials intend to use it to identify noncitizens on state voter rolls, a purpose that several states dispute. The other involves a congressional map that a state adopted, which a lower court found was drawn to favour one party. The justices declined to let the map take effect while the dispute continues. Whatever the Court decides in either matter, the ruling will be read as a statement about the balance of authority between Washington and the individual states.

Much of this work is done at speed, on what practitioners call the interim docket. When a party asks the Court to pause a lower court's order, the justices must act within days. They do so without the full briefing and argument that an ordinary case receives, which makes the outcome harder to predict and harder to justify. Unsigned orders of this kind have become common, and they are increasingly the instrument through which voting rules are settled. Because the reasoning is often compressed into a few pages, or omitted altogether, the public learns what the rule is without learning why. That gap between outcome and explanation is itself a source of suspicion. Several justices have complained about the practice in print, and others have hinted at unease, but no workable alternative has been offered.

Some scholars argue that what matters is not the number of cases but the purpose they serve. A more sympathetic reading holds that courts perform a necessary checking function when electoral administration becomes openly partisan. On this account, the judiciary is unlikely to correct every abuse, and it should not try. What it can do is to identify the most egregious instances and refuse to ratify them. That limited role may prove crucial in the months before an election, and perhaps in the months after it as well. The Court's refusal to disturb the Boston ruling fits this account rather neatly, since the judge relied on the terms of a statute. The distinction matters, because a court that confines itself to the plain words of a law invites less resentment than one that appears to choose a winner. A narrow order that leaves a lower court's judgement intact is a classic instrument of restraint, and it postpones a direct confrontation with the political branches.

Critics of this arrangement respond that every intervention carries a cost of its own. When judges resolve disputes that the political process should settle, they expose themselves to the charge that they are simply another faction in the argument. The result, according to the legal experts who were interviewed this week, is a slow erosion of confidence. Voters who see a rule imposed and then suspended may reasonably conclude that the outcome depends on which side argues better in court. That perception is not new, but it has become easier to sustain as the interval between an election and its litigation has narrowed. The problem is compounded when the same court must rule on several disputes in quick succession. Each decision invites the losing side to test the next rule in turn, and the cycle repeats. Trust, once lost, is difficult to recover, and no judicial opinion, however careful, can restore it by itself.

The deeper cause of the present situation is not judicial ambition but political failure. Legislatures that cannot agree on the terms of an election, or that prefer to write rules favouring their own side, inevitably invite the courts to decide. Until that condition changes, the pattern will persist, whatever the composition of the Supreme Court at any given moment. A modest proposal, advanced by several commentators, is that election administration be entrusted to officials with a measure of independence from the parties they serve. Election officials, not judges, are best placed to weigh the practical consequences of a deadline or a registration rule. Whether such a scheme could survive the pressure of a national campaign is doubtful. The alternative, however, is a system in which every close election ends in a courtroom. Compromise on the machinery of voting is not glamorous work, but it is the only durable remedy available. That prospect should trouble anyone who values the legitimacy of democratic government, whatever their view of the particular cases now before the justices.

title: How environmental change in the Arctic has unsettled both its legal order and its once-cooperative geopolitics
paragraphs: The Arctic has become a subject of intense geopolitical speculation, and it now attracts the attention of lawyers, economists and scholars of international relations as much as that of climatologists. A recent study by Mia Bennett and Klaus Dodds insists that the region's ecological and geopolitical processes are intertwined and cannot be understood in isolation. Their book looks both forward and backward, linking present disputes to the slow development of regional dynamics since the late 2000s. The result is a coherent account of the way physical change alters the legal and political foundations of governance. The title captures this double meaning: the frozen surface is giving way, and so are old rivalries over resources, space and territory. Melting ice, on this view, is not merely an environmental problem but also a legal one, since treaties drafted in a colder era assume conditions that no longer hold. Once that assumption is questioned, the whole structure of Arctic authority appears less stable than it did a generation ago. The purpose of this article is to examine the argument and to assess what it tells us about the prospects for cooperation.

The clearest evidence of the link between nature and law concerns Article 234 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea. That provision grants coastal states special authority to regulate marine pollution within ice-covered areas of their exclusive economic zone. The authors ask how the article should be interpreted if ice covers such areas for only a limited period, or occasionally rather than permanently. As the frozen surface retreats, the geographical facts upon which the rule was based are quietly transformed. Climate change therefore alters the geophysical foundations of the global rules-based system, and it does so without any formal amendment of the text. A similar difficulty affects scientific research on the continental shelf, where data about the seabed may support claims that were previously unavailable. Law, in short, is not a neutral framework imposed upon the region; it is a record of assumptions about ice that are now being tested. This is why legal analysis must proceed alongside ecology rather than after it, and why no court has yet resolved the ambiguity.

The book also describes a long period in which cooperation, rather than rivalry, shaped the region. Growing concern for environmental protection, together with the relaxation of East-West tension in the late 1980s, encouraged the eight Arctic states to work together. Their efforts produced the Arctic Environmental Protection Strategy in 1991, which was absorbed five years later by the Arctic Council, the principal intergovernmental forum in the region. Since 2011 the members of the Council have signed legally binding agreements on search and rescue, oil spill response and scientific cooperation. From 1998 the Council began to admit observers, including European and Asian states with a clear interest in Arctic affairs. Such contacts were hardly new, since Arctic states had traded across the North Pacific long before comparable links with Europe appeared. The result is a region increasingly described as the Global Arctic, a term with both a political and an ecological meaning. Shrinking glaciers, thawing permafrost and rising temperatures affect the entire planet, not only those who live in the far north.

Yet geopolitical ruptures have reduced the appetite of Arctic states for any further expansion of this community. Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, and its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, divided the eight states and eventually brought formal cooperation to a halt. These events have also discredited the hope for Arctic exceptionalism, the view that the region's harsh climate, sublime landscapes and limited infrastructure would persuade states to cooperate. Nearly three decades of faith in that idea produced real benefits in science, environmental protection and safety. Whether such benefits can be sustained now seems doubtful, and at this stage the authors are right to say so. They argue that pan-Arctic cooperation is most likely when Russia, which has the longest coastline in the region, is weak. The collapse of the Soviet Union in the 1990s created precisely such a situation, but since the early 2000s Russia's resurgence has undermined cooperation. Heavy investment in Arctic oil, gas and minerals has served to support Moscow's claim to great power status. The melting that made such extraction possible has damaged the people and the environment of the region. The loss of ice has thus become a factor in its own right.

Militarization plays a part in this process, and it is linked to more than the defence of territory. It began as natural resources became more accessible, and it has accelerated as East-West relations have worsened. The most recent Arctic policies of the eight states emphasise national security and territorial integrity, a shift that risks sidelining the Arctic Council. Sovereignty, combined with proximity to an opening ocean, has become a deeply divisive element in regional politics. In 2008 the five coastal states issued the Ilulissat Declaration in order to assert control over adjacent waters. That statement excluded Finland, Iceland and Sweden, and it reflected a broader anxiety about growing global interest in Arctic governance. The same anxiety has pushed Arctic states to cooperate with various actors outside the region in order to advance their own interests. The agreement to prevent unregulated fishing in the central Arctic Ocean, signed by the eight states together with China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea, illustrates the trend. Because fish are an important global commodity, the regulation of fisheries matters greatly, since warming may shift the distribution of stocks and thus create friction between states.

Disputes of this kind have already appeared in the Svalbard area, where Russia and Norway disagree about access and jurisdiction. Meanwhile, the accession of Finland and Sweden to NATO in 2023 and 2024 has deepened Russia's isolation and hardened the division of the region. Climate change has altered the potential areas of conflict between NATO and Russia on the increasingly open surface of the Arctic Ocean. If the Arctic Council still functions, more now seems to divide its members than to unite them. Russia has responded by turning towards Asia, and towards China in particular, a relationship that may prove decisive. In theory the Council remains in being, but the quality of cooperation it once embodied has plainly declined, and no institutional model has emerged to replace it.

What, then, should be concluded from this account? The value of the book lies less in prediction than in its insistence that ecology and politics belong to a single story. Legal instruments designed for a frozen ocean cannot simply be applied to a melting one, and pretending otherwise will not make the difficulty disappear. Nor can cooperation be restored by declarations alone, since the position of the largest Arctic state determines whether the region is managed collectively or contested. A more realistic approach would accept that competition and collaboration must coexist, and would seek to protect the scientific and environmental achievements of the past three decades. That is a modest purpose, but it is one that the evidence clearly supports, and it is perhaps the most useful lesson the book offers.

title: The cross-border popularity of Pakistani television drama in India and its limits as a force in political relations.
paragraphs: The setting is modest and the budget is small, but the dispute at the centre of the plot is entirely domestic. A young lady has opposed her senior relatives, and her quality as a partner is now in doubt. Two actors perform their lines while a director observes, and in an internal space the owners of the estate wait with their furniture. Within a period of months, a considerable audience will view that furniture, and a good many of them will be viewing from India. The series is one of about a hundred that Pakistan produces every year, an industry that employs several thousand individuals. Realistic setting, natural communication and ordinary plot about marriage have made these dramas popular internationally as well as domestically. The two nations have fought three wars, effected a division of a disputed territory and maintained a hostile attitude now in its eighth decade. Tv, it seems, is succeeding where politics has failed, and it does so without any official support.

The two governments remain opposed on every point that matters, and the list of matters is remarkably limited. For India the central issue is terrorism, while for Pakistan it is the disputed territory of Jammu and Kashmir, and neither side will discuss the complaint of the other. Officials meet, exchange courtesies and return home, leaving the public to form its own conclusions about the nation next door. It is this gap that tv fills, and it fills it without any policy, authority or accord behind it. The programmes cross the border, but not through any channel that a government controls or that a cultural council approves. Indians view Pakistani series on YouTube and on streaming platforms, sometimes with subtitles and sometimes without, and the exchange is entirely private and largely unrecorded. No minister has endorsed it, no treaty covers it, and no official figure measures it. This is not a system that any government designed, and perhaps that is precisely why it works so well. A hundred series a year do not amount to a policy, but they may be the only form of influence that either side can exercise without provoking resentment.

For an older audience the habit began long before the network, when a determined household could sometimes catch a signal from Pakistan's state broadcaster. One author in the Indian city of Patna recalls her mother-in-law and an aunt adjusting equipment in the 1980s in the hope of holding a picture steady. That was her first evidence that the neighbour was a producer of serious drama rather than a source of threat. Two decades later she was viewing the same series with her own daughter, and they had lost none of their appeal. The characters feel familiar to her, and at the same time they offer a relief from ordinary living. A route in Karachi might as well be a route in Lucknow or Patna, and what happens to the people on the screen could happen to her associates. The point is not that the two societies are identical, but that their relations are obvious in a manner that political argument never allows. Transport between the nations is difficult, and for most Indians a tour to Pakistan is an impossibility rather than a proposal. The screen supplies a replacement, offering locations, businesses, facilities and the titles of neighborhoods that a viewer learns to pronounce. Here is a history of the region delivered not by a document but by the sort of domestic detail that a document ignores. After a period of official statement, such direct experience of a neighboring culture is difficult to ignore.

Pakistani drama earns its audience by methods that appear almost anti-commercial by the standards of the region. Indian production is dominated by large budgets and elaborate settings, and its cinema has long been the most powerful in South Asia, yet its series run for years and pad their plots with flashbacks. Pakistani programmes are cheaper, shorter and quieter, and they usually conclude after twenty or thirty episodes. Their plots turn on family living rather than on events, and the writing allows a character to be neither hero nor villain. A viewer in the southern city of Hyderabad remarks that the people on the screen have shades to them. That, in her account, is what makes them human, and it is also what makes them credible. An actor who has worked in the industry since the 1980s puts the contrast plainly, saying that what Bollywood is to India, the series is to Pakistan. He argues that the strength of the form lies in its simplicity, in the quality of its writing and in the discipline of a fixed number of episodes. The result is a product that a whole family can view together, and one that crosses a border that people themselves cannot cross.

The traffic, however, is not symmetrical, and the barriers in the way of the reverse journey are political rather than artistic. Pakistanis have viewed Indian films for decades, but hostility between the governments means that they cannot see them in cinemas, and the bans are mutual. India restricts content from across the border on tv as well, although its own industry is far larger and its audience far wealthier. What Pakistan offers, according to its practitioners, is a form of restraint, with little violence, no vulgarity and nothing that a parent would have to explain. That condition, rather than any conscious strategy, may be the reason Indian viewers find the series so easy to accept. A director in Islamabad reports that his pages fill with comments from India, and that viewers once prayed for the recovery of a character in a coma. The attachment is to the people in the plot, not to the nation that produced it, and that distinction keeps the audience loyal.

It would be a mistake to conclude that such affection can alter the course of policy. The same audience who follow a Karachi family every evening also live in a nation that regards Pakistan as its principal security threat. Trade between the two economies is negligible, and there is little commercial interest on either side. Entertainment does not reduce arms, settle a disputed territory or change a vote in parliament. What it can do, at most, is to complicate a picture that propaganda has kept simple. The author in Patna grew up hearing that the neighbour would take everything from India. The series have since added the kind of detail that propaganda never permits, and doubt begins in precisely that way. Whether such doubt accumulates into anything that could be called political is uncertain, and perhaps it never will be. The directors are doubtful in a different sense, wondering whether audiences in the West would understand lives so unlike their own. Some of them would like their work to appear on international platforms, but they are not confident that it would travel.

For the present, however, the audience that matters most to the industry is the one next door. The governments of India and Pakistan may have nothing to say to each other, but their citizens have found something to view. That fact is small and easily dismissed, but it is also evidence that a shared culture survives a political dispute which has outlived two generations. The dramas are not politics, and nobody involved in making them claims that they are. They are a reminder that the border, however heavily guarded, runs through a region whose habits, foods and family disputes remain common property. An actor in Karachi puts the case with an enthusiasm that no policy document could match, insisting that they are our people and that they eat as we eat.

title: Taryn Simon's Guggenheim installation and the contested nature of American history
paragraphs: The central hall of the Guggenheim Museum in New York has been filled with images about monitoring, deception, violence and international conflict. The exhibition that occupies it is likely to be remembered long after the ordinary collection of exhibitions staged across the nation is forgotten. Those exhibitions, mounted to mark the 250th anniversary of the republic, centered on vague notions of democracy and discontent. Taryn Simon's Father Country I Do Love You is a new 42-part installation that operates at once as a major conceptual art project and as an unconventional form of investigative research. Its central claim, argued through accumulation rather than assertion, is that American history has become chaotic, incomplete and permanently subject to change. The national past, on this account, was never settled, and it was never confined within the borders of a single state. That assumption, the artist suggests, is one that political authority has a particular interest in, since it makes the record of the past appear stable and complete.

The project began in 2017, when Simon encountered an agent's name in files kept by the FBI during the 1990s. She tracked him down, met him at a restaurant in Maryland and established a rapport strong enough to support repeated interviews over a period of several years. She has concealed his identity, partly to create the sense that he could be anyone. The exhibition does describe his life, beginning with his birth in an unknown year at a medical facility in New Hampshire. It continues through his role in international operations run by the United States in nations that include China and Saudi Arabia. Yet the output is less a biography of a single figure than a vast collection of more than 1,000 images, provided alongside thousands of terms of material. Only a section of that text comes from Simon's personal interviews with him.

The collection draws into the agent's orbit an array of individuals and firms, among them a beauty business in Beverly Hills run by a figure in the January 6 insurrection. Others include a summer camp in New Hampshire and the kids who attend it, witnesses to a bombing in Nairobi, and the producer of a particular range of goods. The amount of data is remarkable, and absorbing all of it in a single visit is effectively impossible. That, however, is exactly the point of the whole project. As a result, American history has become difficult to describe in a direct or concise manner. A considerable part of society has become involved in it, willingly or not. Because that history has become widespread, it has also become increasingly difficult for the public to see. Simon often conveys this notion by providing images that appear innocent before revealing themselves to be otherwise.

One array of images, for instance, shows an array of individuals standing around bridges in sunny forests, and in one of them a woman stands near a peaceful brook. A note beneath the image claims her to be a Saudi immigrant who has come to appreciate, as she puts it, how strange her situation is in the grand sweep of history. A nearby text adds that the forest is in Foxstone Park in Virginia. There Robert Hanssen, a double agent operating for the FBI, once left secret messages meant for the KGB. If one follows Simon's logic, the woman is connected to Hanssen, who is in turn linked to the anonymous agent because he apparently monitored an agent working for the Russians. The connections the artist makes are vague, and their details are typically vague, seemingly by design. The evidence for such links, therefore, is not always easy to confirm. Whether we are seeing fact or fiction often does not matter, as the agent himself reminds her. Simon also places his words beside images of the site on Long Island where a TWA plane exploded in 1996 amid a mysterious line of light. Some things, the agent observes, cannot be proven.

That sentiment has run through much of Simon's output since the early 2000s. The Innocents, the project that first achieved her widespread recognition, shot men whom the courts had wrongfully convicted, often at the sites where they were claimed to have committed their crimes. There followed a series of installations that established her signature formula of linking masses of images with explaining text. One of them was the cleverly titled A Living Man Declared Dead and Other Chapters, in which Simon charted an array of lines. It took its name from four Indian men declared dead as part of an inheritance plot even though they were still alive. Visible and invisible, alive and dead, fact and fiction: all have become blurred in an art that seeks to reach the bottom of things. Her obsessive search for truth in the accounts of other individuals is a common impulse among journalists, and it has sometimes seemed to me that her art might better exist as journalism. Is it really necessary to see so many beautifully shot images when the text beside them says well enough on its own?

The Guggenheim project offers a clever solution to that problem by rendering any mere notion of truth obsolete, since the facts as Simon provides them cannot exist in isolation. She seeds the installation with fictions and lies, shooting Jodie Foster, the actress who famously played an FBI agent in The Silence of the Lambs, for one production set near the beginning. The agent claims to have witnessed Foster training for the role at an FBI fingerprinting lab, an accident that seems both impossible and difficult to deny beyond any shadow of doubt. Whether we can confirm any of it, however, feels beside the point, since the majority of us will view Simon's image of Foster with inked fingers and recall her Oscar-winning performance. The artist also turns her lens on individuals whose memories are vague. One is a public affairs officer at the Defense Logistics Agency who, according to Simon's text, repeatedly injured himself and threatened the artist and her crew during a four-hour photoshoot in 2021. In a two-channel video provided here, the man says that he does not recall doing any of that, though he does not exactly dispute her account either. Repeatedly one of the installation's two screens goes dark, as if to mirror all the unretrievable responses that would be needed to explain the encounter.

In the presence of so much misdirection, a clever thought becomes suspicious, and the issues that follow are difficult. What is Simon not telling us? Can she be trusted? Is all of this really connected? The same logic, indeed, might be applied to any official account of the recent past. This, I think, is precisely what makes Father Country I Do Love You so significant. The work produces the sense that the nature of American history is endless, chaotic, incomplete and permanently subject to change. It resists the notion that the nation's past was ever set in stone or confined to the country's borders, as the government intends it to be. "Individuals enter with their account all tied up inside of them," a medical expert who treats individuals of the intelligence community informs Simon. Playing the medical expert to a confused American identity, the artist lets the nation continue to tie itself in knots as it processes 250 years of grief, anger and anxiety.

title: The political economy of public subsidies for sports stadiums
paragraphs: When the Buffalo Bills open their 2026 season in a new stadium, it will be the first of six venues that the National Football League plans to occupy within the next six seasons. The Tennessee Titans will move into a new dome in 2027, and the Cleveland Browns expect to follow two years later. Clubs in Missouri and Colorado have scheduled their own openings for 2031; the pattern is familiar, and so is the bill. When the Bills project was announced in 2022, economists called the public contribution of $850 million from New York State and Erie County a very poor deal. That figure has since been surpassed by later projects, whose public subsidies average more than $1 billion and reach $5.74 billion in total. The Kansas City Chiefs alone have obtained $1.8 billion from the state of Kansas, and the cost of the venue in Denver is not yet known. In every case a substantial part of the expense will be met by taxpayers rather than by the clubs that will occupy the buildings. For many local governments, such a commitment is the largest single item of spending they will approve in a decade.

Researchers have studied the public financing of sports venues for decades, and their findings are remarkably consistent. The economic benefits that host communities receive are far too small to justify the money they provide. A recent book on the subject summarises the evidence: stadiums do not generate growth, because they mostly move existing spending from one section of a city to another. Money spent inside a venue is money not spent in nearby restaurants, shops and cinemas, so the net gain to the local economy is close to zero. Employment at a stadium is often seasonal or part-time, and the posts that appear are frequently offset by losses elsewhere. The same conclusion has been reached by researchers who differ in method and in political view, which makes the agreement hard to dismiss. Any intangible reward, such as the pride that a successful team may inspire, is difficult to measure and rarely large enough to settle the account. Subsidies, in short, transfer money from the general public to a small number of very wealthy owners. Yet the deeper puzzle is not whether the investment pays; it is why elected officials approve it when the research is so clear.

Part of the answer lies in the ordinary cycle of leases and buildings: venues that remain in perfectly good condition are nonetheless replaced roughly every thirty years, because that is the term written into the agreements that clubs sign with city authorities. When such an agreement expires, a team has every incentive to press for a new structure rather than to renew the old one. Public agencies rarely bargain hard in such negotiations, since the alternative appears to be the loss of a team that voters value. The last great wave of construction peaked around the turn of the century; the present increase in activity is therefore predictable, and it will probably continue for another decade. Owners also gain from what economists call the novelty effect: a new venue attracts larger crowds for a time and produces a temporary rise in revenue. The club, meanwhile, moves into facilities of a standard it could not otherwise enjoy, and both sides therefore have reasons to prefer building to renewing, whatever the wider cost to the area may be.

Public money does more than reduce an owner's cost; it also changes the design of the building. When government shares the burden, a team bears only part of the expense while keeping all of the benefit. It therefore builds something larger and costlier than it would choose alone, which economists describe as gold-plating. New venues accordingly contain heated concourses, private clubs and other expensive details that an owner would never pay for out of his own pocket.
