The result is a building whose quality is set by the willingness of politicians to spend other people's money. The Bills' new home, for instance, includes exclusive lounges with fine food and a private whisky locker for supporters willing to pay extra. Even the roof has been designed to melt snow over the majority of the seats, a feature that costs far more than the ordinary protection it replaces.

For a long time economists argued that the monopoly power of the leagues drove these subsidies. By limiting the number of clubs, it was said, owners created competition among cities, and officials had to commit tax money in order to keep their teams at home. That account no longer fits the evidence: the four major leagues have added between three and eleven clubs each since 1990, yet subsidies have continued to increase. If monopoly power were the main cause, the arrival of new clubs and the growth of television revenue should have reduced the pressure on public funds; the opposite has occurred. Many teams have obtained new facilities without ever threatening to leave, and none of the clubs now building a venue has used an offer from another city as an implicit threat. Relocation is discussed in public, certainly, but it is rarely the cause of a decision.

What the public wants, however, is not in doubt: when the question is put to a referendum, voters usually reject it. A review of such votes found that only 58 percent passed, and the successful ones won by an average of just 51 percent. Proposals considered by representative bodies, in contrast, were approved in 96 percent of cases, with an average level of support of 80 percent. Surveys of voters in Nashville and in upstate New York found that majorities opposed the deals offered to the Titans and the Bills. Subsidies do not always fail at the ballot box, since voters in Oklahoma City and San Antonio recently approved new arenas for their basketball clubs. The Kansas City club, having lost a local vote, simply turned to legislators in a neighbouring state where the electorate had no direct say. The Tennessee club spent $1.6 million on lobbying in order to secure approval from representatives rather than from voters. Between 2005 and 2017, only six of 39 subsidy proposals were decided directly by the public; teams have therefore learned that cutting voters out of the process is the surest method of obtaining public money.

Why, then, would a representative support a project that most constituents oppose? It is difficult to know what politicians think, but a few conditions are suggestive: elected officials tend to be male and well educated, and this group is more likely than average to follow professional sport with interest. Teams have openly cultivated lawmakers with play-off tickets and luxury boxes, and representatives often enjoy access to premium spaces that the rest of society never sees. Officials in New York, for example, have been criticised for watching Bills games from a suite that taxpayers helped to finance. A proposal may well seem more persuasive when it is presented over drinks in a private box, surrounded by prominent citizens and a cheering crowd. Those who bear the cost of a stadium are diffuse, while those who receive the benefit are few and well organised. Owners appear to have learned that although they cannot fit a majority of the electorate into the owner's box, there is always room for the members of a city council.

title: The humanities under threat: Australia's Job-Ready Graduates policy and the value of non-vocational education
paragraphs: More than a hundred prominent Australians have signed an open letter whose central demand is quite specific and, in the present political climate, radical. It asks the prime minister to simply abolish the Job-Ready Graduates package and to replace it with a fee structure that does not punish students who choose the humanities and social sciences. The signatories range widely across Australian intellectual life, from a Harvard professor of Australian studies to a musician who once served in a labour cabinet. Novelists, historians and scientists appear on the same list, and several describe the study of literature or history as the very foundation of everything they have since produced. Although the letter was published only this year, the policy it attacks has survived two federal elections and three education ministers, a continuity that makes the signatories' argument very unusually pointed. What they are challenging, in other words, is not just one clause of a statute but a settled assumption of government.

Job-Ready Graduates was simply promoted as a means of guiding students towards disciplines of national need. Under its rules, fees for degrees in science, engineering, education and nursing fell, while the cost of other courses rose quite sharply. Philosophy, history and literature bore the steepest increases: history fees jumped by 117 per cent, and an arts degree now easily exceeds fifty thousand dollars. The scheme did not, however, provide additional places in the cheaper fields it claimed to favour, and actually the number of places awarded in those subjects barely moved. It simply penalised students who seek degrees with less predictable career outcomes, and it thereby produced a very clear message about the sort of knowledge a society is prepared to support. Such choices, on this view, were utterly self-indulgent and economically irrational. The evidence has followed very quickly, indeed almost immediately, for humanities enrolments have fallen to a ten-year low. The architects of the policy assumed that students would simply follow the price signals and choose the cheaper degrees. No movement of that kind occurred at all on the scale projected. What changed instead was the level of debt carried by those who chose the humanities, and that burden falls very hardest on students from poorer families.

Universities, meanwhile, face steadily escalating costs and volatile income from international students, and in that economic context humanities departments are an easy target. At one institution, up to 124 full-time positions are simply being cut as part of a thirty-million-dollar restructure, with heavy losses across the arts. At another, entire majors in sociology and politics are being eliminated, and a third is quietly shedding thirteen humanities roles. These are not isolated incidents but sections of a very broad pattern of disinvestment, a pattern documented in detail by staff unions and local newspapers. The cuts are justified on financial grounds, yet the amounts involved are quite modest in relation to the whole institutional budget. What is truly being judged, however, is value. Humanities faculties appear to return too little for the money they consume, and no committee of management is ever willing to defend them on any other basis. The result is a form of control exercised through accounting rather than through argument, and the authority to decide what counts as useful knowledge shifts quietly towards administrators, almost imperceptibly. Local communities lose not only teaching but the public lectures, archives and research projects through which a university once served its region, and perhaps the most consequential loss is the one often never recorded at all.

Against that accounting, the qualities the humanities produce are difficult to measure and therefore easy to dismiss. Interpretive reasoning, ethical judgement and historical understanding are not products that can be counted at the end of a financial period. Anyone who has taught literature at a university has observed how the study of complex texts cultivates something slower and more deliberative than the transfer of information. A novel that grapples with sovereignty, environmental stewardship and inherited trauma offers no quick answers; it invites a kind of intellectual disorientation which is the beginning of serious thought. A nineteenth-century novel of provincial life, read attentively, becomes a slow education in moral attention, and the same is true of a poem examined line by line. Works of this kind encourage patience, a tolerance for ambiguity and the capacity to hold contradictory ideas at the same time. These are habits of mind rather than mere academic skills, and they are central to the conduct of civic life in any democracy worth the name.

The same method is visible wherever students examine an ancient paradox about identity and change. They may also consider a philosophical argument that frames belief as a rational bet under conditions of uncertainty. Neither is treated as an academic curiosity; both serve as frameworks for judgement and moral reasoning. What is practised here is a mode of learning that has become rare: slow, rigorous and open-ended, requiring nuance, comparison and a tolerance for uncertainty. The poet Keats called it negative capability, the capacity to remain in doubts and mysteries without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. In a public sphere marked by polarisation and misinformation, that disposition is more relevant than ever, and it cannot be produced by any course of vocational training. Reading such material therefore does not merely inform students about the past; it models how to remain intellectually and ethically open when no obvious answer exists.

There is a peculiar irony, and a growing sense of contradiction, in the present situation. History podcasts attract large audiences, philosophy books shape national conversations, and employers and business groups continue to cite communication, judgement and adaptability among the most desirable qualities in graduates. Humanities graduates remain employable across a wide range of industries precisely because they can read closely, write clearly and think critically. When pandemic responses required weighing personal privacy against public safety, or vaccine equity against speed, the skills in play were not only technical but interpretive and ethical. Indigenous-led campaigns for voice, treaty and truth have drawn upon legal frameworks, storytelling traditions and historical understanding, all of which lie at the centre of the humanities. Humanities-trained writers and advocates have played a leading part in reshaping public messaging during successive crises, from climate policy to public health. Change, these examples suggest, is not only engineered; it is narrated, debated and imagined into being. The appetite for large, messy human questions is evidently real, and yet the institutions that taught people to ask them are shrinking.

The universities accord has now accepted that the scheme failed to achieve its objectives and has recommended urgent reform. Yet the deeper problem is not a single policy instrument, and it will not be solved by adjusting one set of fees. It is a failure of imagination, one that reduces education to training for a labour market and measures every form of knowledge by its immediate rate of return. Some learning is valuable because it deepens understanding, sharpens empathy and expands the imagination, and no data set can record that gain. A system that offers only vocational instruction may produce competent employees, but it will not produce citizens capable of weighing evidence and accepting the uncertainty that serious judgement involves. If the current course continues, the loss will be recorded as a saving, and the argument for the humanities will have to be won again from the beginning. To make students ready for work while withholding the tools to reason clearly and imagine ethically is to leave them, in the end, soul-starved.

title: Corporate art patronage, tax deductions, and the public cost of LVMH's gift to the Musée d'Orsay
paragraphs: The Musée d'Orsay in Paris confirmed in January 2023 that it had acquired La Partie de bateau, an 1877 painting by Gustave Caillebotte that critics now place among the major achievements of Impressionism. The price was €43 million, a figure that far exceeded the museum's annual acquisition budget of roughly €3 million. The ministry of culture had already classified the canvas as a national treasure and had forbidden it to leave the country for thirty months, thereby starting a countdown to keep the work in France. Yet the ministry did not release the funds required to purchase it, and the painting might easily have slipped back into private hands. A public appeal for sponsorship followed, and it offered an attractive incentive: a tax deduction covering 90 per cent of the cost. The Louis Vuitton Moët Hennessy group, a long-standing patron of the museum, seized the opportunity at once. Its generosity, however, was largely financed by the French taxpayer, and that fact received almost no attention in the press.

Caillebotte's reputation has followed a curious line. He fell out of fashion before his death in 1894, mainly because the subjects he chose, manual labour and idle leisure among them, seemed out of date to the critics of his period. A century later the same canvases attract museums and wealthy collectors, and prices have risen to a level that alarms public institutions. In 2021 the Getty Museum in Los Angeles paid $53 million for Young Man at His Window, breaking the painter's previous record of $22 million, set at auction two years earlier. Such figures explain why the French state was so eager to keep The Boating Party at home, and why a local museum could never compete on its own. The market, rather than the museum, sets the terms, and those terms have become impossible for all but the richest institutions. A work that was once dismissed as minor has thus become a symbol of national prestige, and prestige, as everyone in this business understands, has a price.

The mechanism that allowed the purchase is not new. Under a law of 2003 on corporate patronage, a business that helps the state acquire a work of art may deduct a large share of its outlay from its taxes. The provision was designed to encourage philanthropy, yet it also allows a firm to convert a marketing budget into a tax saving. When the Louis Vuitton Foundation was built in Paris in 2014, the group reduced its construction costs by 60 per cent through the same provision, a rebate of €518 million. That single project accounted for 8 per cent of the country's tax breaks for the year, and parliament responded by imposing limits on the law for the first time. The arrangement rests on a simple logic: the state obtains a painting, the company obtains prestige, and the cost falls on the general body of taxpayers. Whether this should be described as private generosity or as public expenditure depends entirely on where one chooses to draw the line.

Similar questions surround the donations made after the fire at Notre-Dame de Paris in 2019. LVMH pledged €200 million for the restoration, while insisting that it would not benefit from the patronage law. The claim was technically accurate and practically misleading, since the firm's donation ceiling had already been reached and no further deduction was available in any case. The pledge also served a competitive purpose. Bernard Arnault, the group's principal shareholder, wanted his gift to dwarf the €100 million promised by Kering, the rival luxury group founded by François Pinault. Criticised for the gesture, Arnault broke his usual silence and told shareholders that in some countries he would have been congratulated rather than attacked. The episode illustrates how difficult it is to separate cultural support from corporate rivalry, and how readily the two are confused. Critics who raised the point were accused of ingratitude, which is perhaps the most effective defence available to a donor.

Publicity is, of course, part of the point. The Caillebotte acquisition was announced in an elaborate press release, which then reappeared almost verbatim in a news agency dispatch; the resulting reports described a generous gift to the nation and said nothing about the government's contribution. A private group that uses a painting bought for a public collection as an instrument of advertising invites an obvious objection. The deeper problem is that the taxpayer funds 90 per cent of the campaign. For the company the cost is minimal, the image gain considerable, and the operation may also yield a diffuse influence within the museum itself. Donations, as every fundraiser knows, generate an implicit sense of indebtedness, and a donor who has covered part of the bill may expect a voice in later decisions. Nothing in law prevents this; the structure of the incentive simply makes it likely.

The fate of the painting after its acquisition suggests how thoroughly patronage and promotion have merged. To celebrate its arrival in public collections, the canvas was sent on a tour of regional museums, from Lyon to Marseille and then to Nantes, an unusual practice intended to reach the widest possible audience. Someone then proposed that it travel between cities by boat, along the canals and rivers, since a boating party ought to arrive by water. Paintings are normally moved in crates, by lorry or aircraft, under the supervision of specialist staff; a slow and potentially hazardous voyage for a work of exceptional value makes little sense. The crate itself became part of the story. Louis Vuitton reportedly offered to carry the painting in one of its famous trunks, a proposal that would have secured extraordinary publicity. In the end the curators chose speed and sent the work in an ordinary case, but the company had already won the argument in the press. In 2018, Vermeer's The Milkmaid travelled from Amsterdam to Tokyo in a Louis Vuitton trunk; the trunk did not own the painting, but the association was useful all the same.

What, then, should be made of such gifts? They are neither wholly selfless nor straightforwardly corrupt. They are transactions, and like most transactions they produce effects that no single party fully controls. The French state has chosen to encourage private support for the arts through the tax system, and that choice has consequences: museums gain objects, companies gain reputations, and the public pays without being told. Limits imposed by parliament after 2014 have reduced the most extravagant deductions, yet the underlying principle remains. If the public is to fund the display of its own heritage, it might reasonably ask for a clearer account of who benefits, and by how much. That is not a plea against patronage; it is a plea for transparency, and for a policy that treats the taxpayer as a participant rather than as an unnoticed partner. Patronage of this kind is not unique to France, but the French system makes its arithmetic unusually visible.

title: Technological optimism about shared abundance versus the politics of taxing extreme wealth
paragraphs: Elon Musk recently assured an interviewer that by 2036 money will no longer matter. Within a decade, he predicted, robots and artificial intelligence will supply more food, housing, transport and entertainment than any human could possibly consume, scarcity will be all but eliminated, and a condition of incredible abundance for all will follow. Retirement saving, he added, will shortly become irrelevant. The claim is striking chiefly because the person making it controls more wealth than any individual now living, and because his fortune did not arise from abundance at all. It arose from ownership of assets, from privileged access to capital markets, and from sustained public support. Musk's forecast therefore raises an obvious question that his own pronouncements never answer: through what political and institutional mechanisms will the output of intelligent machines be translated into a general improvement in living standards?

Musk is not alone in his faith. Mark Zuckerberg has published a philosophical statement arguing that superintelligence, once available to everybody, will generate gains in productivity and economic growth that ultimately benefit everyone. The venture capitalist Marc Andreessen goes further, insisting that there is no conflict between capitalist profit and a social welfare system that protects the vulnerable, since the money created by markets pays for everything else people want. What these manifestos share is a conspicuous silence. Each describes, in lavish detail, the abundance that technology will produce; none describes how that abundance will be distributed, or who will decide.

The three men differ in temperament and in the details of their forecasts, yet they share an assumption that is rarely stated plainly: that distribution can be left to the market. When pressed, they tend to fall back on a familiar claim, that growth itself eventually raises living standards for everyone. The historical record offers only partial backing for this view. The industrial revolutions of the past two centuries did raise average incomes enormously, but they also produced long periods of extreme concentration. The gains were widely shared only after bitter struggles over wages, hours and taxes. Nothing about machine intelligence suggests that its rewards will flow more easily or more evenly than those of the steam engine.

Distribution, it turns out, is not a technical matter but a question of power, ownership and political arrangement. This is the argument advanced by Gabriel Zucman, an economist at the Paris School of Economics and a leading authority on wealth and taxation, whose recent book examines how the ultra-rich minimise their obligations and what might be done about it. His central proposition is deceptively simple: wealth does not distribute itself. However impressive the productive capacity of artificial intelligence becomes, existing political arrangements will continue to concentrate its rewards in very few hands.

Zucman does not merely assert this; he quantifies it. Across Europe, the United Kingdom and the United States, he finds, those at the top of the wealth distribution pay virtually no tax on their earnings. The method is familiar to anyone who follows financial journalism. Billionaires shelter their money inside personal holding companies, retaining profits rather than taking them as salary, while their fortunes grow through unrealised capital gains that no authority taxes. Wealth expands, power expands, and taxable income all but disappears. The French data make the pattern unusually vivid. Taxation there is broadly progressive across the vast majority of the population: working-class households pay an effective rate of about 45%, the middle classes about 50%, and the upper classes slightly more. At the very top the pattern reverses, with the rate falling to 13%; measured by income tax alone, the ultra-rich pay roughly 2%.

The phenomenon is not peculiar to France: similar calculations for the United States and several northern European countries reveal the same inverted structure, in which the effective rate falls as wealth rises. Part of the explanation lies in the mobility of capital, which allows fortunes to be moved across borders. Another part lies in the complexity of modern corporate structures, which permit earnings to be turned into a form no tax authority can easily reach. Large firms and rich individuals alike have learned to exploit the gaps between national fiscal regimes. The resulting competition for capital has steadily weakened the ability of governments to levy progressive taxes. Each new avoidance scheme is met, after a delay, by a new regulation; each new regulation, in turn, breeds fresh schemes. The race is unequal, because the private sector commands far greater resources than the bodies meant to police it.

The implications go well beyond fiscal bookkeeping. Large-scale tax evasion has been one of the central mechanisms behind rising inequality and mounting government debt, and it has encouraged many people to abandon any expectation of a fairer society, a disillusion that supplies fertile ground for reactionary movements. Extreme wealth, on this account, reproduces itself, and those who possess it deploy considerable resources to make an unequal status quo steadily less equal. It is worth emphasising what Zucman is not proposing. He does not seek to abolish billionaires, nor does he advocate absolute economic equality; the charge of far-left activism, levelled by one of the richest men in France, misreads a case that is democratic rather than socialist. Democracy, he contends, requires that citizens be treated equally under the law, and the tax practices of the ultra-rich violate that principle.

History offers some encouragement. In the decades after the Second World War, many Western countries levied rates on the very rich that would now seem confiscatory, and they did so without stifling growth or destroying incentives. The top marginal rate in the United States exceeded ninety per cent for much of the 1950s, and in Britain it was similarly high. Those rates were not always effective, since rich people found ways to conceal their money even then, but they expressed a broad consensus that extreme inequality was dangerous to democracy. That consensus has since eroded, and with it the fiscal capacity of the state. Zucman's minimum tax is best understood as an attempt to rebuild a fragment of that consensus in a world where capital moves far more freely than it did in the 1950s.

His remedy follows from the diagnosis. Because the earnings of the very rich arrive as corporate profits and rising asset values rather than as salary, income tax cannot reach them. What is required instead is a minimum annual tax of 2% on fortunes exceeding one hundred million dollars, a levy calculated to offset the regressive features of the present framework. The sums involved are large, yet the burden is modest in relative terms. Billionaire fortunes grow by roughly 6% a year, so taking a third of that growth would leave the richest people in the world comfortably the richest people in the world, while closing the door on avoidance strategies based on holding companies, trusts and shell companies. The proposal is therefore not an act of confiscation but a condition of democratic fairness, and it is grounded in evidence rather than prophecy.

There is a particular irony in the fact that the most enthusiastic prophecies of shared abundance come from men whose fortunes demonstrate the opposite. Technological innovation has generated extraordinary riches, but that wealth has not spread through society; it has produced a new class of ultra-billionaires and, before long, trillionaires. Citizens are invited to trust in a future of infinite plenty while the institutional arrangements that would distribute it remain unbuilt. Zucman's contribution is to insist that the question is political, answerable through law and taxation rather than through technological optimism, and that the choice between concentrated and shared prosperity will be made by governments, not by machines.

title: The U.S. Supreme Court's criminal docket and why it should accept more cases to resolve lower-court conflicts
paragraphs: The Supreme Court opens a new term with a docket in which criminal law and related cases occupy an unusually large share of the whole. By one recent count, eleven of the twenty-five cases already granted review raise questions of criminal law and procedure, a proportion close to forty per cent. That figure would be striking in any period. It is more striking still when set against the court's shrinking overall output, for the justices now hear argument in fewer than sixty cases a term, less than half the number they handled a generation ago. The supply of unresolved legal questions, meanwhile, has not diminished at all. The court therefore has both the opportunity and the obligation to accept more criminal cases, especially those in which lower courts have reached conflicting conclusions on points of federal law. Such conflicts create uncertainty throughout the criminal justice system, and the cost of that uncertainty is borne by local police, by prosecutors and by defendants alike.

Last month the Congressional Research Service published a lengthy report on circuit splits. It listed almost a hundred instances in which the federal courts of appeals have disagreed about significant questions of statutory or constitutional law. The largest single category by far was criminal law and procedure, which accounted for twenty-eight of the disputes, roughly three times the number in civil procedure, the next largest group. The questions at issue are hardly trivial. Does embezzlement count as a continuing offence that extends the period within which a prosecution may be brought, and is carjacking a violent felony when the relevant state statute also reaches extortion? Is criminal forfeiture limited to property that a defendant has actually acquired, and what degree of intent must be established before a violation of civil rights can be proved? Each of these matters affects the liberty of individual defendants, and each remains unsettled because no authority above the circuits has resolved it. The report offers no opinion on how such disputes should be settled, but it confirms that the differences are real and that they persist from one year to the next.

The capacity to decide more cases is not in doubt, and neither is the legal basis for doing so. In 2012 Chief Justice John Roberts observed that the court could hear a hundred cases a term without any stress or strain. He emphasised that disagreements among the lower courts were by far the most important consideration in deciding whether to grant review. That view has been repeated often since, and it remains central to the argument for a larger docket. The court's own rules point the same way, identifying a conflict between courts on an important federal question as a reason for accepting a case. National uniformity on questions of federal law was, after all, among the oldest reasons for establishing a single supreme court. That principle matters most in criminal cases, where the stakes include personal liberty and where a single disputed point of law can determine the outcome of thousands of prosecutions. Yet the justices continue to accept only a small fraction of the petitions that reach them, in part because they exercise almost complete control over their own docket. The resulting uncertainty imposes real costs on defendants, prosecutors and the police alike.

Consider the most conspicuous item on the term's criminal calendar. Several states and one large county prohibit the possession of what their statutes call assault weapons, a category defined to include semi-automatic rifles such as the AR-15. The question whether a legislature may ban an entire class of widely owned firearms has been building for years. The solicitor general has now asked to take part in the argument, a sign of how much the executive branch wants the matter settled. The dispute turns on a phrase in the 2008 decision that first recognised an individual right to keep a handgun for self-defence. That opinion rested on a bare majority of five justices, and its author listed various longstanding prohibitions that he left undisturbed. He then added a further limitation: the weapons protected by the Second Amendment, he wrote, were those in common use at the time the amendment was adopted. The qualification was almost certainly necessary to hold the majority together, and it therefore ought to be treated as part of the binding judgement of the court.

The government's brief in the case, however, quietly alters that language. It proposes a different test: whether such rifles are in common use today, rather than whether they were in common use when the amendment was ratified. The difference is not merely verbal. Semi-automatic rifles were first sold in 1903, and the AR-15 was developed in 1956, so neither could have been in common use at the founding. Their present popularity is a product of modern engineering, and it is precisely that novelty which makes them attractive to those who seek them. Two justices adopted the revised phrasing when they dissented from a denial of review, and their choice of tense suggests that they are prepared to read the earlier limitation out of the opinion altogether. If a majority follows them, the practical effect will be to convert a narrow ruling into a broad one without any explicit overruling. The court would thus have changed the scope of a constitutional right while claiming merely to apply it.

Other cases on the calendar raise questions of comparable importance, though they are unlikely to attract the same publicity. One asks whether a jury in a serious criminal trial must consist of twelve members rather than six. The answer is likely to come not from a close reading of the constitutional text but from an appeal to a long tradition. Yet the ruling will bind every court in the country. Another case asks whether the seizure of an aircraft, as punishment for the unlawful transport of a small quantity of beer, amounts to an excessive fine of the kind the Constitution forbids. Taken together, these disputes illustrate how much of the court's criminal work consists not of headline cases about rights and liberties in the abstract, but of technical questions. Their resolution determines whether a prosecution may proceed, what evidence may be used and how severe a penalty may be imposed. In each instance the practical effect of a ruling will be felt far from the courtroom, in the ordinary business of law enforcement.

The court's reluctance to grant review cannot be explained by any shortage of qualified petitions, and it cannot be excused by a lack of capacity. What is missing is a settled sense of priority, together with a willingness to accept the additional work that a larger docket would bring. Criminal law therefore deserves a more prominent place on the docket than it now receives, for such questions are most numerous in this field and the consequences of disagreement are most immediate. The same conduct may be treated as a serious crime in one part of the country and as no offence at all in another, which is a situation no legal system should tolerate. Nothing in the public interest is served by leaving important federal questions open to divergent answers. The justices need not decide more cases in order to decide more criminal cases. They need only choose differently among the petitions that reach them, and thereby restore a measure of uniformity to a body of law that affects the liberty of every citizen.

title: Two new books trace Australia's twenty-first-century leadership instability to a series of structural shocks that its major parties failed to grasp.
paragraphs: Australian politics has acquired a reputation for instability that few comparable democracies can match. Since the turn of the century the country has been led by seven prime ministers, one of whom held the office twice. A rate of turnover of that kind would once have been thought extraordinary in a system built on stable two-party competition. Two recent books, one by an award-winning political journalist and one by an academic historian, seek to explain how this happened. Although they differ in method, they arrive at a common diagnosis. Both identify a sequence of structural shocks that the main parties failed to recognize in time, and both describe a governing class that remained suspended in an imagined past. Neither author is greatly interested in personality, and each treats the rapid removal of leaders as a symptom rather than a cause. The real subject of both volumes is institutional failure, an inability to respond to changes in the electorate, in the workforce and in the wider world. The first is a study of leadership in the twenty-first century; the second examines the social and economic forces that constrained it. Both present themselves as the conclusion of a trilogy, which suggests that the argument has been under construction for some years.

The first of the three shocks is demographic, since for the first time since federation Australians of migrant background and their children form a majority of the population. The established parties have been slow to absorb that fact, and the second shock concerns employment, where professional women have replaced blue-collar men as the largest section of the workforce. The third is international, because the allies and trading partners on whom the country has long depended have proved unreliable. Labor has adapted to all three more successfully than the conservative coalition, and the independent crossbench, drawn largely from professional women, better still. The electoral effect became visible in the defeats of 2022 and 2025, when voters of migrant background deserted the coalition in marginal seats. One author offers the image of a family tree, with indigenous roots, an old Australian trunk and new Australian branches. The first shock, he argues, arrived at the moment when the branches became larger than the trunk. He also proposes a line, named after an Indian cricketer, that separates the cricket-loving Indian suburbs of Melbourne from the football-obsessed towns of Geelong. Conservative prime ministers who grew up in Sydney, he observes, all came from its least Eurasian districts.

The politics of gender has shifted in ways that the coalition has found especially difficult to manage. For much of the country's history the conservative parties were more popular with women than with men, but by the time of the Morrison government that advantage had reversed. One prime minister appointed a single woman to his first cabinet, and the first female leader the Liberals eventually chose was tolerated for only nine months. Their opponents have done considerably better, since a majority of Labor's parliamentary party are now women. Women also head public institutions that had never previously been led by them, including the central bank and the Productivity Commission. The community independents who won formerly safe conservative seats embodied the same movement, and family background may help to explain the difference in approach. Two conservative leaders were the dominant figures in households where fathers set the tone and the sons attended single-sex schools. The current prime minister, by contrast, was an only child raised by a single mother and a grandmother, and his style is collaborative rather than commanding.

The third shock is embodied in the person of the American president, who inspires less confidence among Australians than any world leader except those of Russia and North Korea. Both the United States and China have broken trade agreements they made with Australia. The assumption that great-power protection is available at a modest price no longer holds. Climate policy illustrates the cost of delay more clearly than any other area of public life. Before the 2007 election both the incumbent prime minister and his challenger promised to introduce emissions trading, and for a time it appeared that the argument, like the science, had been settled. It had not, because climate change became entangled in cultural conflict and was used as a weapon against three successive leaders. That conflict contributed to the end of all their tenures, and Australia remains the only country to have removed a price on carbon. The consequence is a foreign policy conducted without the reassurance of a dependable protector, and a domestic debate in which the value of expertise is easily dismissed as self-interest.

The record on economic policy is similarly discouraging: the mining boom of the early years of the century should have offered an opportunity to repair the tax base. Instead, taxes were cut in a manner that could not be sustained, and later governments continued those reductions while proving unable to offset them with lower spending. A national scheme of disability support was established without adequate provision in the budget, whether through a broader revenue base or through cuts elsewhere. Subsequent administrations then allowed public spending to drift above the levels Labor had produced during the global financial crisis. Productivity growth has slowed markedly, and the rapid expansion of private consultants, who displaced experienced public servants, has been described as an expensive disaster. The consequence is a state whose capacity has been reduced at the very moment when the demands placed upon it have increased. The political debate seldom reaches these structural questions, and indeed the quality of the argument suffers accordingly. A country that cannot raise the revenue it requires will struggle to meet the expectations of an ageing society.

Judging leaders while they are still in office is a hazardous business, and the verdict on the current prime minister must wait. Of the others, only John Howard seems likely to appear in lists of successful leaders. His legacy is mixed, since he undermined the tax base during the boom and prepared to price carbon before abandoning the idea. None of his successors achieved the most basic measure of political success, which is re-election, and three of them were not even permitted by their parties to attempt it. The prime minister who emerges worst from both accounts is Scott Morrison. He appointed himself to five ministries without informing the public. He spent a fortune on a detention center built for arrivals who never came, and went on holiday during a national emergency. One author calls his administration the most odious of the century, though such verdicts are inevitably personal. The nature of the underlying problem is structural, since a system that rewards short-term survival will keep producing leaders who cannot address the shocks that have shaped the country. The alchemy of leadership, on this evidence, lies less in the qualities of individuals than in the willingness of parties to adapt before events force them to do so.

title: Disaster preparedness and the myth of technological rescue
paragraphs: The devastating hurricane season of 2005 completely destroyed the comforting myth that a modern urban city can manage any emergency through better technology alone. Emergency planners had long assumed that superior forecasting would translate almost automatically into efficient and timely action, yet the evidence from the Gulf coast suggested otherwise. When a storm of truly exceptional strength approached the coast, officials issued detailed warnings several days in advance, and yet hundreds of thousands of vulnerable residents remained in their homes. The failure was not one of prediction but of capacity, of trust, and of money, as subsequent investigations made clear. Researchers who studied the event concluded that a warning is merely a message until a community possesses the means to respond to it. That conclusion has since been confirmed across a wide range of disasters, from wildfires in Australia to floods in northern Europe and Asia. The central problem, in short, is not the accuracy of the forecast but the ability of a society to act upon it. Preparedness, once regarded as a purely technical matter, has therefore become a test of social and political will.

That test is often failed, and the consequences are especially severe for those who can least afford to lose their homes, their savings, or their lives. In the case of the 2005 storm, the authorities had the data, the models, and the satellite images, and they had the legal power to order an evacuation. What they lacked was the capacity to move the elderly, the poor, and the sick, who had no cars, no money, and no safe place to go. The failure was therefore not a failure of science but a failure of social provision and of political priority. The same pattern appears repeatedly in other disasters, both recent and historical. During the 2003 heatwave in Europe, thousands of elderly people died alone in flats without air conditioning, even though meteorologists had predicted the extreme temperatures several days in advance. In Australia, the Black Saturday bushfires of 2009 killed 173 people, many of whom had received warnings but chose to stay and defend their property. In each case, the warning was clear, but the ability to act was not equally distributed across the population.

This is why the study of disasters has shifted from a focus on natural hazards to a focus on social vulnerability. A hazard becomes a disaster only when it intersects with human systems that are already under strain. The poor, the elderly, the disabled, and racial minorities are consistently more likely to die, lose their homes, and suffer long-term economic damage. The reasons for this pattern are structural rather than accidental: poor people often live in low-lying areas that are prone to flooding, in housing that is poorly built and inadequately maintained. They may lack insurance, savings, or access to transport, and they may not have the social connections that help others to escape. They may also distrust government warnings, having learned from experience that official promises of help are not always kept. This distrust is not irrational; it is a reasonable response to a history of neglect and broken assurances. Thus, any serious policy must address not only the physical infrastructure of protection but also the social infrastructure of trust and mutual aid.

The role of government in this process is therefore central, but it is not unlimited. The state can build levees, enforce building codes, and fund emergency services, yet it cannot coerce every citizen into safety or force people to listen to its advice. It can offer shelters, but it cannot guarantee that people will use them when the moment comes. The most effective strategies combine technical measures with community-based ones that draw on local knowledge. Local residents often know which routes flood first, which neighbours need help, and which rumours are false. Churches, clubs, and informal networks can spread warnings and organise rescues faster than any central authority, in ways that no official agency can easily replicate. In the aftermath of the 2005 hurricane, for example, ordinary people in small boats rescued hundreds of their neighbours while official agencies hesitated. This is not to romanticise volunteerism or to excuse government failure; it is to recognise that disaster response is a collective enterprise in which formal and informal institutions must work together.

A further complication is that the frequency of extreme events is increasing across the globe, as climate change raises sea levels, intensifies storms, and extends droughts in many regions. At the same time, more people are moving into vulnerable areas, often because housing is cheaper there. The result is a rising level of risk that no amount of forecasting can eliminate. We can improve our models, but we cannot predict every accident, every failure of equipment, every human error; what we can do instead is reduce our exposure and increase our capacity to adapt. That means investing in infrastructure that is resilient, in social security that protects the poor, and in public education that teaches people how to prepare. It means treating preparedness not as a one-off campaign but as a constant feature of daily life. It also means accepting that some risks can never be eliminated and that we must learn to live with uncertainty.

The psychology of risk also deserves careful attention from policymakers and emergency planners. People often ignore warnings because they have never experienced a disaster, because they believe that bad things happen to other people, or because they fear that evacuating will lead to looting and loss. These are not simply individual failings; they are predictable responses to uncertainty, and effective communication must therefore be repeated, consistent, and delivered through channels that people already trust. A message from a neighbour or a local doctor may be more persuasive than a statement from a distant official. The authorities must also be honest about what they do not know and about what they cannot promise. False confidence can be more dangerous than admitted uncertainty, because it discourages people from taking their own precautions. Building a culture of preparedness requires a long-term relationship between citizens and the institutions that govern them, a relationship that depends on trust.

Ultimately, the lesson of the 2005 hurricane and the many disasters that followed is that technology is a tool, not a solution. It can enhance our ability to see a threat coming, but it cannot by itself create the will or the means to escape it. A society that invests only in forecasting while neglecting its poor, its elderly, and its infrastructure is building a house on sand. The measure of a community is not how many satellites it can launch but how it treats its most vulnerable members when the floodwaters rise. Preparedness is therefore an act of collective responsibility, a test of whether we are willing to protect one another. If we fail that test, the next disaster will not be natural at all; it will be a man-made catastrophe, produced by our own refusal to confront the social causes of suffering. The choice is ours, and it is a political choice as much as a technical one. We can continue to pretend that better gadgets will save us, or we can build a society that is genuinely resilient.

title: The escalating tariff dispute between the United States and the European Union over spirits, and what it reveals about the costs and politics of trade policy.
paragraphs: When one government concludes that another has treated its exports unfairly, the obvious answer is to impose a heavier tax in return. That logic, however crude, has shaped American trade policy for a long period, and it has produced a series of decisions whose effects reach far beyond the industries they claim to protect. The current dispute between the United States and the European Union over spirits provides a particularly clear case in point. At its centre is a threat to place a duty of 200 per cent on wine, champagne and other alcoholic products entering America from Europe. The threat appeared within days of a European decision to tax American whiskey at 50 per cent. On the surface, however, this looks like a narrow quarrel about one type of goods. In fact it involves questions of power, of national interest and of the relationship between politics and the market. It also raises a practical issue that economists have described for centuries: who actually pays when a government decides to tax what its citizens buy from abroad? The general answer, in almost every case, is the consumer.

The general sequence of events is easy to describe. Within the past month the American administration has conducted a tit-for-tat campaign against its largest trading partners, among them Mexico, Canada, China and the European Union. Its stated aims are to reduce the flow of drugs across the southern border and to persuade manufacturers to move their operations home, thus creating more American jobs. Duties of 25 per cent were imposed on steel and aluminium entering from thirty-five countries. Europe replied with taxes on American exports worth 28 billion dollars, and Canada added measures of its own on goods worth 20.7 billion. Canada also asked the World Trade organisation to consider the matter, a step that may lead to a formal legal process. European measures will apply not only to metals but also to textiles, household appliances and agricultural products. Motorcycles, bourbon, peanut butter and jeans are included as well, much as they were during an earlier period of conflict. Officials in Brussels have been explicit about their method: they have selected goods from states where political support for the current administration is strongest, so that the pressure falls where it is likely to matter most.

This approach has consequences that are easy to overlook: spirits producers, who had no part in the dispute over steel, have become collateral damage. The European Union is a major destination for American whiskey, and exports increased by 60 per cent over a period of three years once an earlier set of duties was suspended. The head of the industry's trade association described the new European taxes as deeply disappointing, and argued that they would undercut years of effort to rebuild a valuable market. He added that the two sides had maintained zero-for-zero duties on spirits since 1997, and he urged both governments to bring the quarrel to an end. His appeal — "we want toasts, not tariffs" — expresses a view that a large part of the industry shares. What it does not explain is why a sector that had reached a workable arrangement should now be treated as a weapon. The answer lies in the nature of the policy itself, and in the fact that its effects are never confined to the goods it names. When trade measures are used to apply political pressure, the goods chosen are selected for their symbolic value rather than for any economic logic. Bourbon from Kentucky and motorcycles from Wisconsin matter because of the states in which they are made, and not because of the cost they add for consumers.

The costs of this strategy, however, do not disappear when the threat is withdrawn. Economists generally agree that a duty is a tax, and that the importing company passes most of it on to the consumer. The result is higher prices in the shops, a narrower range of choice, and a transfer of income from households to the public purse. Research on earlier tariff episodes has found that the burden falls hardest on poorer families, who spend a larger share of their income on goods of this type. The effect on employment is smaller than politicians claim, because protection allows inefficient firms to continue while it raises costs for everyone else. The stock market appears to have reached a similar conclusion. The three main American indexes have fallen sharply, and the broadest measure ended one day more than 10 per cent below its recent high. The Treasury Secretary dismissed the fall as a little volatility over three weeks, and said that his attention remained fixed on the real economy. That distinction is difficult to accept, since financial markets are part of the real economy and determine the cost of capital, and therefore the investment on which future output depends.

There is also a question of law, and of the system that governs international trade. Since the middle of the last century, governments have accepted a framework of rules designed to prevent exactly this sort of escalation. That framework does not forbid retaliation, but it requires that any response be limited in both range and effect, and publicly justified. Whether a duty of 200 per cent can be defended under those rules is doubtful, and the dispute process that Canada has set in motion may eventually produce a ruling. Yet the deeper weakness is not legal but political: a system that depends upon the restraint of its most powerful members cannot continue to function when restraint is treated as weakness. The same difficulty appears within the United States, where the argument has moved from economics to identity. A leading business newspaper observed that most citizens understand duties to be a tax on consumers and businesses; the administration replied that the paper's thinking was antiquated and weak. Once a question of policy is reframed as a test of loyalty, evidence ceases to matter.

What, then, should be made of the threat against European spirits? It is tempting to treat it as a temporary episode, a bargaining position that will be abandoned once concessions are offered. That reading may prove correct in the short run. But the wider pattern deserves attention, because it involves a shift in the way governments understand their role in the economy. For much of the post-war period, trade was regarded as a means of increasing wealth for all participants; it is now increasingly described as a contest that one side must win. This change has real effects on investment, on prices and on the relationships between countries that have long been close allies. It also creates a problem of credibility: a government that threatens its partners repeatedly will find that its offers are worth less, and that the agreements it signs are harder to enforce. The spirits producers, whose exports depend on predictable rules, are the first to feel that loss, but they will not be the last. Perhaps the most useful lesson is a modest one. Trade policy is a part of government, not a substitute for it, and the interests it serves should be stated openly rather than disguised as a defence of the national interest.

title: Museums and scholars are reframing colonial histories, and the reckoning demands evidence rather than gestures.
paragraphs: For much of the past two centuries, the great national museums of Europe presented their collections as monuments to universal knowledge rather than as products of conquest, trade and unequal exchange. Visitors had little reason to ask how particular objects had arrived, and still less to ask whose labour had produced them. That arrangement is now under pressure, and the pressure comes from several directions at once. Scholars, students and the governments of formerly colonised states have begun to demand a full account of provenance, the documented record of an object's ownership and movement. Institutions that once treated such questions as marginal now find them central to their public position. The result is a series of exhibitions and books that do not merely add new material to a familiar narrative, but rewrite the narrative itself. The strongest of these projects are not gestures of apology, because they change the evidence upon which a museum's authority rests.

The British Museum's exhibition Ancient India: Living Traditions offers a case in point, since it gathers some 180 objects drawn from its own collection and from international loans. Sculptures, paintings, drawings and manuscripts trace the spread of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain devotional art across Asia over more than two millennia. The route runs along the Silk Road towards east Asia and across the Indian Ocean towards south-east Asia. What matters most, however, is that the display seeks to highlight provenance. The religious traditions of ancient India were plural and overlapping, and their history requires narration of a high quality if it is not to collapse into caricature. For a long period, institutions in London and Paris told that history as a story of discovery, in which European scholars were the main agents and Asian practitioners supplied the material. Curators now accept that the record does not support such a view. The museum is at least beginning to acknowledge the post-colonial reckoning that cultural institutions can no longer ignore. Whether that acknowledgement will extend to the restitution of contested objects remains an open question, and the answer will depend less on scholarship than on law and politics.

A comparable exercise in reframing is being conducted at a much smaller scale, and largely online. The Welsh community of Patagonia, known as Y Wladfa, was established almost two centuries ago. Its founders hoped to preserve a language and a culture that seemed to be losing ground at home. In the process, a small country that had itself been colonised became a coloniser. The Indigenous Tehuelche people helped the incoming settlers to adjust and adapt to an unfamiliar environment, and they have since been marginalised in the record of the settlement. A digital exhibition marking 160 years since the first arrivals restores some balance of perspective. It presents the experience of the Tehuelche and challenges the widespread notion that the largely peaceful coexistence of the two populations was due to Welsh benevolence. The claim is not that the settlers were unusually cruel, but that a story told from one side only is an incomplete and therefore misleading form of history.

The most ambitious contribution to this debate comes from literary criticism rather than from the museum world. In The Trembling Hand, the comparative literature scholar Mathelinda Nabugodi examines a period that is usually discussed in terms of freedom. By the middle of the nineteenth century, as slavery was being abolished across much of Europe and the Americas, romanticism had spread through art, literature, music, philosophy, science and political argument. Its central ideal was an exalted notion of human freedom. Yet that ideal is rarely considered in relation to the slavery question, although the two were bound together in fact as well as in logic. Nabugodi shows how the proceeds of slavery underpinned literary production, and how received ideas about race permeated European culture in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Her chief purpose, however, is to make the presence and the contribution of black people visible in a history from which they have been systematically removed. Universities have responded to calls to diversify the curriculum, and a new canon of black romantic writing is beginning to be taught. Nabugodi insists, nonetheless, that examining the ideas of race and slavery built into the traditional canon matters more than adding texts beside it.

The transformation is visible in education as well as in galleries, and it is there that it may prove most durable. Departments of history and literature are revising the courses they offer, and publishers are responding to a demand for texts that were once considered peripheral. A programme of this kind depends on research, and research depends on records. Where archives were destroyed, or where the only surviving documents were written by officials who had an interest in distortion, the process of recovery is slow and uncertain. Scholars must apply to scattered sources a method that can yield reliable results, and they must be willing to report what the data will not support. The quality of the argument, rather than the prominence of the author, decides whether a claim about the past will hold. That is a condition of any serious academic project, and it applies with particular force to a field in which political pressure is strong. The main risk is that a new canon will be assembled as carelessly as the old one, and then defended with the same intolerance.

It would be a mistake to treat this reckoning as a settled matter, or to assume that it proceeds at an even rate. Museums depend on public funding, private donors and government policy, and each of these imposes its own conditions, economic and political, upon what may be said. Governments that are unwilling to accept criticism of their own national record are unlikely to welcome a critical account of a colonial past. There is also a genuine intellectual issue, which has nothing to do with bad faith. The evidence available for the history of a marginalised people is often thin, scattered and recorded by their opponents, so a revised narrative may rest on inference rather than on proof. Scholars must therefore distinguish between what they can demonstrate and what they can only suggest. The danger is that institutions, eager to appear enlightened, will substitute the vocabulary of decolonisation for the labour of research. A label that announces a reckoning, without changing the material it describes, offers the appearance of change and the substance of none.

What distinguishes serious work from performance is the willingness to accept a loss. A museum that publishes a full provenance record may find that some of its most prized objects can no longer be displayed in good conscience. A scholar who traces the money behind a literary career may find that a beloved reputation will not survive the discovery. These are real costs, and the institutions that bear them are producing better history. The reframing of a colonial past is not, in the end, a matter of taste or of political fashion. It is a question of accuracy, and accuracy is the only basis on which a museum, a university or a book can reasonably claim authority. The alternative is a form of collective forgetting that presents itself as scholarship, and that the next generation will have every reason to reject.

title: Harriet Taylor Mill's neglected contribution to political philosophy, and the case for restoring her to the canon
paragraphs: Few figures in nineteenth-century political thought have suffered as much from the neglect of posterity as Harriet Taylor Mill. Her influence on John Stuart Mill, the most celebrated British philosopher of his age, was for a century either denied or openly dismissed. The evidence now available, however, suggests that she was an original thinker in her own right. She was a radical critic of marriage, of education and of the position of women, and the author of arguments that her husband later made famous. Her case therefore raises a general question about how the history of philosophy is written, and about who is allowed to count as a philosopher at all.

Her only solo-authored essay published in her lifetime, The Enfranchisement of Women, appeared in 1851. In it she asked why women were still regarded as mere appendages to men, without interests or purposes of their own. Her answer was characteristically blunt: the only reason that could be given, she wrote, was that men liked it. More than twenty years before On Liberty, the work with which her husband is usually associated, she had already outlined the principle that would make that book famous. Every human being, she argued, has a right to all personal freedom which does not interfere with the happiness of some other person. That claim, which later became known as the harm principle, is normally attributed to John Stuart Mill alone. Her arguments were consistently on the side of independence, and her sympathies lay with the powerless and the oppressed. The value she placed upon independence followed from a particular view of human nature, in which the capacity to choose was central.

She also diagnosed the central political and economic question raised by the industrial revolution. It was whether the condition of the poor should be regulated for them or by them. Her views amounted to a programme of reform that would be considered radical even today, let alone two centuries ago. She called for secular schools and universities, for complete freedom of speech, and for all occupations to be equally open to men and women. Such measures would require a government willing to act against established interests, and no such government existed in her lifetime. She demanded strict limits on the amount that any individual could inherit. Marriage, in her account, should be like any other partnership, dissoluble at pleasure. With language that was often witty and pithy, she cut to the heart of issues in political thought such as patriarchy, social justice and freedom.

In the 1830s, while caring for three young children from her first marriage, she wrote for the Westminster Review on a wide range of political and philosophical subjects. Her essays ranged from colonialism in Australia to Plato, and her criticisms were always pro-democratic and anti-aristocratic. She also produced many unpublished articles on the social and economic structures which left women vulnerable to abuse and exploitation by their husbands. In the 1840s and 1850s John Stuart Mill and Harriet Taylor wrote a series of excoriating newspaper articles on violence, especially domestic abuse. They attacked the unwillingness of the courts and the police to act against it. They pointed, too, to the inequalities of power which rendered people in subordinate positions so vulnerable to brutality. Perfect equality was her ideal, in politics, in the workplace and in the home. But by equality she did not mean equality of outcome; she endorsed a system of reward based on effort and talent rather than inheritance, and called for a higher standard of justice. Her insistence that the higher the kind of enjoyment, the greater the degree of pleasure it yields foreshadowed the distinction between higher and lower pleasures that her husband drew three decades later.

Despite her lifelong commitment to fighting injustice, her contribution to her husband's work has largely been ignored by the scholars who followed. Mill himself often tried to give credit where it was due, but his earliest attempts were blocked by her first husband, who feared the attention that their unconventional relationship would attract. When they eventually married in 1851, Mill attempted to renounce the power and control over his wife that the law of marriage would grant him. He recorded a formal protest against that law, and repudiated any pretension to have acquired rights by virtue of it. Later he catalogued in his autobiography how many of the works published as his own had in fact been his interpretations of her ideas. He republished The Enfranchisement of Women under her name, and corrected correspondents who congratulated him on a work that was not his. Curiously, his desire to praise her became, in the hands of later critics, an excuse for ignoring her.

One essay published shortly after Mill's death complained that men had been blinded by affection and bewitched by womankind. In the view of such critics, his love for his wife had clouded his judgement of her intellectual capacities, in which he had been entirely deceived. A hundred years later this myth acquired a Freudian twist, and Mill was said to have chosen her because she shared his mother's first name but his father's personality. As recently as 2022 a biography argued that Mill, brought up in a totalitarian micro-state by his father, needed someone else from whom to take orders, a claim that other academics have refuted as misogynistic. Taylor Mill may well have expected such treatment in the years after her death in Avignon in 1858. But in the twenty-first century it is time that she were recognised as an incisive and influential thinker in her own right. Such evidence matters because the canon of western social philosophy is not a neutral record of achievement. It is the product of a long series of decisions about which texts are worth preserving, and those decisions have usually been taken by men. Women who wrote anonymously, or whose work appeared under another person's name, were especially likely to lose their place in it. The tendency is not confined to philosophy; it affects every area of intellectual life in which reputation depends on public acknowledgement.

Perhaps the most striking feature of Taylor Mill's thought is its refusal to treat the freedom of women as a separate cause. The claim rests on the same principle as everyone else's freedom: that individuals should be allowed to develop their own capacities, within limits set by the equal claims of others. She understood that injustice damages the whole community, not simply its immediate victims. Her arguments were never purely theoretical; they shaped practical campaigns, from the reform of marriage law to the extension of education to women. Some of these campaigns required decades to produce results; others have still not succeeded. If her name appears less often than it should, the reason lies not in the quality of her work. It lies in the conditions under which women wrote, and in the willingness of later scholars to accept a convenient story. Restoring her to the centre of the tradition would change how that tradition is described. It would provide a more accurate account of where some of its most influential ideas came from. It would also explain why so many of her proposals remain relevant to current policy debates. A discipline that forgets its own critics is likely to misunderstand the ideas it claims to preserve. Harriet Taylor Mill's case suggests that the history of political thought still has work to do.

title: American public opinion on proposals to reform the Supreme Court
paragraphs: For much of its history, argument about the Supreme Court of the United States followed a predictable course. Critics on the losing side of a major decision complained that the justices had overreached, and defenders replied that the court was merely interpreting the Constitution. Any political attack upon the court, they argued, would damage an institution whose value lay in its distance from ordinary politics. That comfortable arrangement has come under increasing strain over the past decade. A series of contentious rulings, together with a steady decline in public approval, has produced a whole range of proposals for changing the structure of the court and the conduct of its members. Approval now stands at one of the lowest levels recorded in half a century of polling, and the figure has been falling for some time. A national survey conducted by a university law school provides some of the clearest evidence available about what ordinary Americans actually think of those proposals. The results are striking, and in one respect they cut against the assumptions of both political parties.

The survey examined three specific ideas, each of which has been debated in Congress and reported in the press. The first is a strict code of ethics, binding on the justices in the same way that it binds other federal employees. Support for this proposal is close to universal: eighty-nine percent of those questioned favored it, and opposition was confined to a small minority. The second idea, a fixed term of eighteen years rather than a lifetime appointment, attracts almost as much approval. Nearly four fifths of respondents endorsed it, a figure that has barely moved across several surveys. The difference between those two results is wider than any plausible margin of error, and it has proved remarkably stable. What divides the public, by contrast, is the size of the court itself, a question on which no neutral ground exists. A proposal to add justices drew support from fifty-three percent and opposition from forty-seven. On this question, therefore, the country is almost evenly split, and the margin is small enough to shift with events.

That pattern is not as strange as it first appears, and the logic behind it is worth setting out. An ethics code and fixed terms can be presented as neutral measures, applying to any justice regardless of which party appointed him. Their effect would be to make the court more accountable without immediately altering the balance of power within it. A voter who distrusts the court may still prefer remedies that do not hand an advantage to the other side. Changing the number of justices is a different matter altogether. It would deliver an immediate advantage to one side rather than to both, and voters understand this perfectly well. The survey data therefore suggest that public opinion follows a coherent logic rather than a random mixture of unrelated attitudes. Where a reform can be framed as a question of process and principle, support is broad. Where it touches the distribution of power, opinion divides along much the same lines as the electorate itself. Republicans and Democrats disagreed sharply about expansion, yet they agreed about ethics, and that combination is what gives the results their interest.

The decline in overall approval, from forty-seven percent to forty-three over two months, deserves separate attention. The change is modest in absolute terms, but it occurred among Republicans and Democrats alike, which is unusual. Ordinarily, a controversial decision damages the court mainly in the eyes of the party that lost the argument. Respondents were also asked how far they trusted the justices to decide cases on legal rather than political grounds, and here the numbers were lower still. When approval falls in both camps at once, the cause is likely to lie elsewhere: in a sense that the institution is no longer functioning as its defenders claim it should. That the fall was equal in both camps is the detail that matters most, because it rules out a simple explanation based on disappointed partisanship. This is the point at which the dispute stops being about this or that ruling and becomes a question about the court's standing in a democratic society. Fifty-three percent in favor of expansion is not a mandate, and forty-three percent approval is not a collapse.

None of this means that the reformers are right, and the strongest arguments against them deserve a fair hearing. Life tenure was designed to insulate judges from electoral pressure, and that purpose has not lost its force. Its defenders claim that any fixed term, however long, would gradually expose the court to the very forces it was meant to resist. An ethics code, they add, is easy to state in general terms and difficult to apply in particular cases. A statute that might look harmless on paper may be used to harass justices whose opinions are unpopular. The machinery of enforcement, they warn, may itself become a weapon in the hands of a hostile majority. Any change to the design of the court, they insist, should be judged by its long-term consequences rather than by its immediate appeal. These are serious objections rather than mere excuses, and any honest account of the debate must contain them.

A recent dispute over official papers illustrates how a technical question can acquire political weight. Justices work for the government, yet they have long treated their official papers as private property, withholding them from the public for decades or destroying them altogether. The administration has cited that practice in arguing that presidents should enjoy the same freedom, and that a law requiring White House documents to be preserved and disclosed violates the Constitution. Whatever the legal merits, the argument depends on a claim about ownership that most citizens would find surprising. It also supplies the reformers with a useful example, since it suggests that the court's own habits, and not merely its rulings, are open to question.

A second theme from the same period bears directly on the first, and it complicates the case for reform. A sitting justice, speaking at a university, warned that Americans do not understand their own system of government well enough to keep it. She cited the reply attributed to Benjamin Franklin, who, when asked what the Constitutional Convention had produced, is said to have answered: a republic, if you can keep it. Her concern was not that citizens disagree about the court, but that they lack the knowledge required to disagree intelligently. If that diagnosis is correct, the debate about reform is a symptom of a deeper condition, and no adjustment to the structure of the judiciary will cure it by itself. Schools have reduced instruction in civics, public discussion has moved to platforms that reward outrage, and the shared vocabulary in which constitutional argument once took place has grown thinner. Civics, once a required subject, now competes with courses that seem more immediately useful to parents and employers. A survey can tell us what people think; it cannot tell us how firmly they hold their views, or how much they understand of what they are being asked. The evidence on reform is therefore best read as one section of a wider record, in which confidence in every major institution has fallen over the past half century.
